en: *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra-vyākhyā*, Scroll One.

Composed by the Venerable Zhanran of Jingxi. Translated by the later student Xuanzhu, with the *Haiyan* (Ocean Eye) commentary by the Tiantai śramaṇa Shiju, and proofread by the later students Xin, Yi, Dazhen, and [others].
The *Shiming Shiyi Shu* states: "Jingxi established that insentient things possess Buddha-nature precisely to manifest the Perfect [Teaching], wherein delusive defilement is itself Buddha-nature;
this is a secondary refutation of the partial pointing toward pure *tathatā*.

Based on this, it can be seen that Siming had already exhausted the intent behind the composition of the *Jinbi*. Therefore, at the beginning of this text, beneath the title, he first demonstrates the "piercing of the film."

In the latter part of my *Zhì* (The Essential Meaning), I addressed the fragmented doubts regarding partial and expedient teachings, subsequently demonstrating the intent of the "wild guest" from the outskirts;

furthermore, in the latter part of the *Shìdì* (The Meaning of the Śrīmālā-sūtra), I first clarified the correct principle of Buddha-nature, having previously discussed this with the wild guest during a quiet night.
By this, one may know that the beginning and end of these works are precisely intended to reveal that delusive defilement is itself the Buddha.
The single character "rigid" (gang) in the sense of "nature" (xing) represents the biased attachment of the Pāñcālaka school;
it causes those who study the Mahayana within the Shanjia tradition to be deluded by their view that insentient things lack nature, thereby causing them to lose the principle of universal endowment.
Therefore, within the context of "nature," the text points out that its substance is all-pervasive.

The Diamond Scalpel (using a round golden blade to excise the film of ignorance from the four eyes, so that everywhere one may see the finger of the *Tathāgatagarbha* Buddha-nature; may the doubts regarding biased expedients be shattered and supplemented by deletions;
entrusting this to a dream of a guest, establishing host and guest—may those who observe it grant their forbearance).
The three dots of the circle-ī (oṃ) are neither vertical nor horizontal, serving as a metaphor for the perfect fusion of the three virtues.

This Great Teaching reveals that the essence of Buddha-nature pervades the four eyes and the two wisdoms, encompassing the myriad phenomena in their dense array. Within the Buddha-eye of the *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing wisdom), true emptiness is profoundly still and silent.
Although the sentient beings of the nine realms possess the four eyes, because their ignorance has not yet been shattered, their Buddha-nature does not manifest.

By means of the Great Teaching of the three virtues of the circular letter *I*, one pierces the cataracts of ignorance of the four eyes within the nine realms, causing the Buddha-eye to open and clearly perceive the wondrous essence of the Buddha-nature.

Once the nature of the nine realms and the three lands has been revealed, the nine realms are themselves Vairocana and the three lands are themselves the Land of Quiescent Light; thus, the term "all" encompasses the ten realms.

Therefore it is said that the person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) immediately penetrates the three paths of the nine realms and perceives the pervasive substance of the three virtues of the Perfect *i* (the letter *i* in its circular form).
The subsequent passage also states: "What in all the worlds is not subsumed? This meaning is based on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says:
"At that time, the skilled physician used a golden scalpel to remove the film from his eye; he first pointed at it with one finger and asked: [The text continues with the physician's question.]
He asked, "Have you seen it? He replied, "I have not yet seen it. [The Master] then removed the film of view and thought to show him the finger of the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
He asked again, "Have you seen the Middle Way, the truth realized therein? He replied, "It is entirely ignorance. [The Master] then pointed it out to him with two fingers.

He asked, "Have you seen it? He replied, "I still have not seen it. [The Master] then removed the film of the *śata-śāhasrika* (dust-like) delusions to show him the finger of the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Pointing to one who has not yet seen the Middle Way, it is said that this is still ignorance; furthermore, he points it out to them with three fingers.
He asks, "Do you see? and they reply, "I see it slightly. This is because the film of ignorance is pierced to reveal the finger of the *Śākyamuni* (Dharmakāya) Buddha-nature and the Middle Way.
Since those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) partially shatter ignorance and partially realize the Middle Way, it is said that they "see it slightly. Thus says the *Fuxing*.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* (Niepan shu) states: "Since it is used as a metaphor for Buddha-nature, it should not be interpreted otherwise; rather, the three truths are taken as the three fingers.
The first finger is like space, hence it is said 'not seen'; the three fingers are like the Ten Abodes, hence it is said 'seen slightly'—this refers to the perfect Ten Abodes.
Through such an opening and resolution, one knows that the four eyes are themselves the Buddha-eye, and that ignorance is [the Buddha-eye]."

The Buddha-nature of the nine realms is itself the Buddha-realm; emptiness and the provisional are themselves the Middle Way. What single dharma is there that is not the *Sāṃbhogakāya* (Saṃbhoga) Buddha-nature?

Although the perfect *Ī* possesses the three virtues, it is precisely the discourse on the one. That the *Sāṃbhogakāya* is the Middle Way within the one is precisely the principle of being three while being one.
If one knows that the essence of the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*) pervades the three and one, and that their aspects are mutually identical, what need is there for further inquiry?
It is not that [the teaching] does not pervade all; rather, it is because other schools are deluded by the partial and expedient teachings within the scriptures.
Now, by directly revealing the perfect and real Buddha-nature, the doubts regarding those partial and expedient teachings are extinguished. Therefore, it is likened to a diamond:
wherever it is applied, there is nothing it cannot shatter. Indeed, because their fundamental tenets differ, [the author] did not wish to protect the prevailing sentiments of the time.

Because I am directly refuting [your views], I have provisionally used the metaphor of a dream and a guest to establish the roles of host and guest; those who read this book must not hold me in fault.
Therefore, I say "I grant you this"—these are merely words of humility.

Since I have been unworthily immersed in the Buddhist scriptures for many years, there has never been a time when the meaning of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) has not occupied my thoughts; I fear that I may not...
To understand that the Great Teaching of asceticism was established for this very purpose is the common path through which all branches flow and the destination to which all currents converge;
it is the great principle of all dharmas and the goal toward which the cultivation of practice aspires.

However, the teaching of Buddha-nature embodies the principle of universal pervasiveness; were it not for those who have applied themselves with deep concentration and accumulated learning, one could not attain a thorough understanding.
Having immersed oneself in the Buddhist scriptures for many years—is this not the result of accumulated study?

Never failing to keep the meaning of Buddha-nature in one’s heart—is this not the result of deep concentration? By means of these two qualities, the texts concerning *nirvāṇa* and Buddha-nature can be mastered.
To explain this further: if one realizes this Buddha-nature, it can serve as the foundation for teaching and practice;
because teaching and practice take this as their basis, they transcend all doctrines and do not fall into false views. Next, the analogy is raised:

the common path corresponds to the general principle, and the ultimate destination corresponds to what is expected. Thus, the teaching elucidates the source of Buddha-nature, demonstrating that it is inherently present within sentient beings.

Just as water originates from a source, it is called the "universal path"; as it proceeds from cause to fruit and moves toward the ultimate fruit, like a stream returning to the sea, it is called the "destination.
If one contemplates this and observes it accordingly, then ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness; form and fragrance are extinguished and purified, even in the Avīci hell.
The entirety of the environment and its inhabitants, and the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage, do not exceed the single thought-moment of even the lowest ordinary person.

This is the phrase that "receives from above. If one can understand the principle of Buddha-nature as described above as the foundation of teaching and practice, then one will realize that all phenomena are none other than the Three Thousand [Realms]; what single dharma would not be the Buddha?
The meaning of the inherent completeness of nature (*xingju*) has never, for even a single moment, transcended the three thousand realms.

What was stated above—that one is indiscriminately bathed in the Buddhist scriptures—means that hearing it is the wisdom of hearing (*wen-hui*), being able to contemplate it is the wisdom of reflection (*si-hui*), and being able to observe it is the wisdom of cultivation (*xiu-hui*);

these are precisely the three wisdoms of hearing, reflecting, and cultivating. If this is so, how could there still be any distinction between ordinary beings and sages, or between form and fragrance? Furthermore...

Although the environment and its inhabitants are spoken of separately, in reality, the environment and its inhabitants are interfused. As for the "ordinary and sagely," some speak of them as the six ordinary beings and the four sages;
however, since the subsequent text refers to the nine grades of rebirth, this [classification] does not correspond to a division into four or six.

Although it speaks of "form and fragrance," the six sense objects are included therein. Because Buddha-nature is one, it is called "one suchness" (*eka-tathatā*); thus, one form and one fragrance are likewise one.
There is nothing that is not the Middle Way; because it is free from defilement and obstruction, it is called "obliterated purity.

From the *Avīci* hell upward, the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) of the Buddha-realm encompass all nine realms. Although this is explained with reference to the lowest realm, it is called *Avīci*.

Since the body and land of Vairocana encompass the nine realms below, and since these nine and the one mutually contain and mutually pervade each other’s environments and inhabitants, this is precisely the "three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa-trisāhasra*).
Although the *Fahua wenju* does not explicitly mention the "three thousand," the essential meaning of the three thousand is contained therein.

Thus, from the phrase "the environment and inhabitants of Avīci, down to the Buddhas, are fully endowed with the three thousand dharmas" to "from the body and land of Vairocana, down to ordinary beings, they are fully endowed with the three thousand dharmas"—it is simply this single reality of the three thousand.
Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind each fully possess these three; there is no distinction between them.
These four phrases serve as the foundation for the subsequent refutation and establishment of the Buddha-nature according to other schools.

Following the refutation and establishment based on this profound principle of the "three thousand [realms] in a single moment" in the text below, the "Wild Guest" (Yake) finally understands the merit of our school’s established "inconceivable realm" of the "three thousand in a single thought-moment," and thus begins his inquiry, asking: "How is this so?"
Although the "three thousand" are not explicitly mentioned here, the essential meaning of the three thousand is contained within it.
Once, during a still night, I contemplated this for a long time; my reflections did not cease, and suddenly, as if falling asleep, I felt as though I were dreaming.
"Inanimate things possess Buddha-nature.

In order to manifest the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) and refute divergent arguments, Jingxi established the metaphor of sleep and dreams to express his views and introduced the "rustic guest" to pose questions.
All these were expedients to clarify the principle through phenomena, artfully establishing a dialogue and provisionally setting up host and guest in a state of mystical resonance.
It was like sleep, yet not actual sleep; therefore it is said, "vaguely as if asleep.
While still in this dream-like state, he suddenly saw a man who said, "I am a rustic guest. His appearance was coarse and rugged, and his movements were erratic.
He approached and stood level with [the practitioner].
The following section refutes the calculations of externalists. "Wild" (*yě*) is a term used to disparage; "guest" (*kè*) conveys the sense of being outside [the fold].
This means that prior to realizing the Buddha-nature, one’s appearance and demeanor are like those of a wild guest;
such is the description of their condition. Because they have not yet deeply penetrated the perfect principle, they are unable to abide in gentleness and goodness.
Because he follows the path of conformity, his demeanor appears coarse and rugged;
because he does not maintain the fundamental course, his coming and going, his advancing and retreating, lack a firm basis, and thus his acceptance and rejection appear inconsistent.
Desiring simply to vie for parity and race alongside the present [master], he is said to "press forward and stand level."
He said to me: "Just now I suddenly heard that you, O Benevolent One, have stated that insentient things possess Buddha-nature. I replied: "Indeed.
He intended to use the doctrines he had inherited, along with the passages from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that refute such views, to challenge the established tenets of our school;
therefore, he first defined its fundamental principle, saying, "Just now... and so forth. My reply, "Indeed," was a general acknowledgment.
The guest said:

"I have respectfully sought out the teachings of Śākyamuni and briefly investigated their fundamental source. The flourishing exposition of this school surely does not surpass the ultimate discourse on the final teaching delivered at the twin śāla trees.
Yet you say that Buddha-nature does not refer to insentient things; why do you alone claim it does not exist?"
Is there any basis for this?

I have respectfully sought and briefly investigated it, and my words are merely humble. Others take *nirvāṇa* as the ultimate teaching; they base this on the ancients’ establishment of *nirvāṇa* as the fifth period of the teaching.
They claim that while the *Lotus Sūtra* discusses how all wholesome deeds return to the same source, it has not yet reached the "pair" [of the two truths].
The Buddha-nature of the trees is the ultimate proclamation; therefore, it is now said: "How could it exceed [the teaching at] the Twin Trees?
Since Nirvana states that tiles and stones lack Buddha-nature, why do you alone claim that insentient things possess it?
I replied: "The ancients even spoke of icchantikas; it is not surprising that they speak of 'insentient things' (wuqing).
However, when the teachings are divided into Great and Small Vehicles, their statements differ greatly. If one says they are insentient, one should not say they possess nature;
if one says they possess nature, it would be inconsistent to call them insentient."
The ancients also spoke of "icchantikas being without [Buddha-nature]," referring to those who maintain that there is nothing in the three realms and nothing in the two vehicles;
they were saying that icchantikas lack Buddha-nature. If this were the case, it would follow that sentient beings also lack Buddha-nature.

Thus, your claim that insentient things lack nature is not particularly strange. This is merely how it was understood by the ancients; however, if we consider it according to the teachings of the present school:

Distinguishing between the "small" and the "great," their assertions differ greatly. This distinction between small and great should be determined by the partial and the perfect, as stated in the following passage:
"The three vehicles of the *āgama* and *vaipulya* have both not yet received the nature-taught [teaching]; what the beginners of the distinct [teaching] receive is not yet complete.

Therefore, these seven types of people may be said to lack insentient [sentience], but it is not said that they lack the Buddha-nature. Only those of the perfect [teaching] know from beginning to end that the principle is non-dual."
Outside the mind there are no objects; who then could be considered insentient? Thus, the statement that "insentient things lack nature" pertains to the three previous teachings;
it is provisional and represents a limited understanding of the insentient as lacking nature. The teaching that "insentient things possess nature" belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Although the four teachings are not explicitly mentioned here, their meanings are contained within this. As for the meaning of the passage below regarding the "wild guest," one should fully understand its significance.
He then asked, "I have heard of the four teachings upon which you rely; may I hear your interpretation of their meanings?

The guest replied, "The *Nirvāṇa* section is vast; why are they all listed together? I said, "It is because you are not conversant with the presence or absence of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), nor with the provisional and real aspects of the teachings and sections, that you doubt this like an ordinary person."

This text arises from the division of the aforementioned teachings into Great and Small. If one were to say that the Great [Vehicle] excludes insentient things and *nirvāṇa*, would this not contradict the Great Teaching?
Why then are insentient things and Buddha-nature listed side by side? The "Wild Guest" (Yekè) was unaware that the essence of Buddha-nature is all-pervasive;

Jingxi, however, examined the matter by distinguishing between the Great and Small Vehicles according to their respective doctrines. Regarding this point, the Wild Guest again clings to his own sectarian position.

"Difficult to instruct" refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Since this is a major division [of the teachings] and is of great scope, it can only be categorized as "great" for those with the Buddha-nature (*gotra*).

Why, then, is the "small" category of insentient beings also listed? Jingxi [Zhanran] criticized this point because [the text] failed to understand the provisional and real aspects of the teaching divisions regarding the presence or absence of Buddha-nature.
This is because although the *Nirvāṇa* division is a major section among the teachings, it discusses [Buddha-nature] within its midst.
The teachings comprise both the provisional and the real; therefore, the Buddha-nature has its degrees of advancement and deficiency. Thus it is said:

because you, my son, are not conversant with the advancement and deficiency of the Buddha-nature, nor with the provisional and real aspects of the teaching sections, you have come to doubt [the Dharma] as being equal to that of ordinary people.

Why is this? The *Nirvāṇa* section belongs to the stage of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), yet within that section, when discussing the teachings, there are both provisional teachings—small in measure—and real teachings.
In the Great Teaching of the Mahāyāna, the *正因佛性* (direct cause of Buddhahood) is said to pervade all places; this is termed "provisional" within the context of the *權教* (provisional teaching).
In contrast, the *緣了佛性* (conditional and consummate causes of Buddhahood) are restricted to sentient beings; this is termed "denial.

Because you do not contemplate that the teachings discussed in the various sections of the canon include both the provisional and the real, you cling to the provisional *緣了* and find it difficult to accept the real *正因*. Thus, you harbor doubts regarding the *正因* of the Real Teaching (*實教*).
Because [the Buddha-nature] pervades all tiles and stones, it is doubted by ordinary people. For now,

I shall extensively cite the scriptural texts for your sake, so that those in future generations who wish to cite this text as proof that Buddha-nature is not insentient may well grasp the intent of the sutras,
remain unconfused regarding the nature of reality, and recognize that what I have established accords perfectly with the core tenets of the scriptures.

Now, for your sake, I shall extensively cite the provisional passages from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* concerning the non-pervasiveness of the conditional and consummate causes (*pratyaya-bhāva* and *niṣpanna-bhāva*) as evidence that Buddha-nature is not absent in insentient things.

By doing so, you will well grasp the intent of the provisional teaching regarding the non-pervasiveness of the conditional and consummate causes, and you will not remain ignorant of the tenet of the true teaching—that the essence of the primary cause (*hetu-bhāva*) is all-pervasive. Thus, you shall understand the essence of the primary cause of sentient beings as I have established it.
This is entirely consistent with the tenet of Buddha-nature as discussed in the sūtras.
Now, establishing that the essence of the primary cause (hetu-pratyaya) of sentient beings is all-pervasive, the sūtra text also uses empty space as a metaphor for it;
thus, the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, chapter thirty-one, states: "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space; it is neither internal nor external. If it were either internal or external..."
How can it be said that [the Buddha-nature] exists in all places? Consider the single character "existence" (you): what does space not encompass?
Thus we know that the scriptural text does not permit [the Buddha-nature] to be exclusively internal or external; hence it says "neither internal nor external," and further states "like space.
Since it speaks of the "Buddha-nature of sentient beings," how could this not be the rational nature as the primary cause?
The establishment of the pervasive nature of the true cause of sentient beings was formulated by Jingxi [Zhiyi].
The scriptural text also employs the analogy of empty space, which accords with the central tenet of the sutra. The sutra takes the eternally abiding Buddha-nature as its primary theme;

because the essence of this Buddha-nature pervades all places, it is compared to empty space. The textual passage using the metaphor of empty space appears in the Kāśyapa-parivarta, concerning the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.
The nature is neither internal nor external, just as space is neither internal nor external.
The Buddha-nature originally exists within the minds of sentient beings, pervading all places without obstruction; therefore, space is used as a metaphor.
That which is illustrated by the Buddha-nature is not restricted to the interior of the mind, nor is it restricted to the exterior of form; it can illustrate how space itself is not restricted.
This "internal" is not restricted to that "external. If it were restricted to both internal and external, how could it be called "existing in all places"?
Now, let us ask the guest from the wilderness to observe the word "exists" (*asti*) within the sutra: what does empty space not encompass?
Therefore, the scriptural text does not permit restricting [existence] solely to the internal mind nor specializing it to external form; for this reason, it is called "neither internal nor external."

Regarding the statement that "in all external locations there is [the Buddha-nature] and so forth," and that "Buddha-nature is like empty space," since it is said that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, is this not the rational mind?
This possession of the rational nature is neither internal nor external; it is precisely the Middle Way and the True Cause.

Therefore, it is said: "Is it not the rational nature, the True Cause? As for what is called "Buddha-nature," it is called "nature" because it is the cause; it is not called "Buddha" because it is not yet the fruit.

The term "nature" (*xing*) refers to the nature of the person who will attain fruition, as they already possess it; thus it is called "Buddha-nature. In Jingxi’s works, this is termed the "correct cause" (*zhengyin*) of sentient beings;
in the scriptural texts, it is termed the "Buddha-nature" of sentient beings. In Jingxi’s works, it is termed "pervasive in essence" (*ti bian*);
in Kāśyapa’s [work], it is said to be "like empty space. Since it is stated that Buddha-nature is fundamentally all-pervasive, why...

The reason for provisionally establishing [the threefold truth] now lies simply in this: the "guests from the wilds" (outsiders) know only the provisional teaching, wherein the conditions (*pratyaya*) and fulfillment (*pariniṣpatti*) are restricted to sentient beings, while they do not know that in the ultimate teaching, the essence of the true cause (*hetu*) pervades even tiles and stones. It is said that [the truth] is established because they do not know this.

Although it is called "true and pervasive," it does not merely refer to the Middle Way principle; fundamentally, there are three kinds of threefold principles, and these three principles are originally pervasive throughout both the realization of nature (*xing*) and the cultivation of practice (*xiu*).
The third [nature] is also universal, yet it serves merely as the *vijñapti-hetu* (perceptual cause);

because the mind has not yet been awakened and the causal conditions have not yet been applied, although the nature possesses all three [aspects], it remains in a state of delusion. Thus, when opened, it becomes unified;

therefore, it is simply designated by the common name "the rational nature" (*tathatā-svabhāva*) and the "true causal nature. All sentient beings possess this true nature, which corresponds to the following passage: "This is entirely the rational nature. (3)

Because [the three stages] such as "not yet having resolved the mind" are identical, the outsider fails to understand this meaning and instead explains them according to the provisional teaching’s *pratyaya* (condition) and *hetu* (cause);
therefore, they use the *pratyaya* and *hetu* to challenge the true [teaching].
Next, Kāśyapa asked, "What is meant by 'being like empty space'? The Buddha then answered with the unimpeded state of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
Is this not precisely because the true cause and its fruit are non-dual?
However, the essence of the Buddha-nature is fully endowed with all dharmas; it is neither internal nor external, pervading empty space and equal to the Dharma-realm, without any obstruction.
For this reason, in the thirty-first fascicle, the Kāśyapa Chapter, the Tathāgata uses empty space as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature.
This was because Kāśyapa’s provisional capacity did not understand the intent behind the metaphor of empty space pervading all things; therefore, [the Buddha] proceeded to...
In the thirty-third fascicle, a question is raised: "How is it that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is said to be like empty space?
For now, I shall briefly cite but a single sentence from this inquiry.

This was the cause for the questioning, as Kāśyapa not only failed to understand the Buddha-nature which serves as the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), but also failed to understand the empty space which serves as the object of comparison (*upamāna*). At that time, the Tathāgata [addressed him] who was deluded regarding the reality and clung to the provisional.

To reveal that the true teaching’s correct cause and fruit are non-dual, [the Buddha] does not answer with the cause, but rather answers by means of the matter of the unimpeded interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) at the stage of fruition. Zhiyi (Jiāshāng) classifies this passage as follows:
"Buddha-nature is like space. This text has three sections: first, it clarifies that Buddha-nature is identical to space and is not subsumed within the three periods of time; second, it clarifies...
"Buddha-nature is identical to empty space, neither internal nor external. Later, it is clarified that Buddha-nature is identical to empty space and is without obstruction.
Now, [the text] answers Kāśyapa’s question regarding the "unobstructed state of the fruition stage" by addressing the fruition through the cause.

This is because Kāśyapa’s provisional capacity caused him to be deluded regarding the facts of the fruition while being confused about the principle of the cause; since he has now attained understanding, [the Buddha] speaks of the fruition.

The question regarding whether the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the cognitive-condition (*vijñāna-pratyaya*) of the *asaṃskṛta* (unconditioned) exist was answered by the Buddha through the fruit of Buddhahood. Kāśyapa then raised the objection that because the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) severs the fruits of both the fruit and its objects, all such conditions must be *saṃskṛta* (conditioned).

The Buddha responded that the metaphors of emptiness and the metaphors of phenomena are not identical; thus, Kāśyapa concluded that the Tathāgata, the Buddha-nature, and Nirvāṇa are *bhāva* (existent).
"Should space also be considered existent? The Buddha first answered by following the question, and subsequently clarified the core principle regarding emptiness.

First, he followed the question: "Is that which is not Nirvāṇa called Nirvāṇa? That which is 'not Nirvāṇa' refers to conditioned phenomena and afflictions. Is that which is not taught by the Tathāgata called the Tathāgata?
That which is 'not the Tathāgata' refers to icchantikas and those of the two vehicles. Is that which is not Buddha-nature called Buddha-nature?"
Regarding what is said to be "Buddha-nature" or "not Buddha-nature"—referring here to walls, tiles, and rubble—I now ask:

if these bricks and stones are eternally not [Buddha-nature], are the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) likewise eternally not [Buddha-nature]? Therefore, one knows that the scriptural passage employs provisional teaching (*upāya-deśanā*) to speak of three antidotes;
it temporarily speaks of the three existences (*tri-bhava*) in order to refute the three non-existences.

In this great sutra, the text is arranged into sections to demonstrate that the Buddha-nature is distinct from empty space. Regarding this, the commentator first sets forth the intent of the objection before citing the passage.

Kāśyapa raises a challenge by citing all three dharmas—cause, effect, and the path—because the Tathāgata answered with respect to the effect while intending to reveal the non-duality of cause and effect; thus, Kāśyapa used the effect to infer the cause.
Because both cause and effect exist, [the opponent] raises three dharmas to challenge the analogy of empty space;
since the existence or non-existence of the dharma and the metaphor are not equivalent, the Tathāgata accordingly answers in accordance with the question by means of these three.

Thus the Master of the Record begins his exposition, stating that Kāśyapa refers to the two dharmas of the fruit of the severance through expedient wisdom—that is, the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata—and this is precisely the "fruit of fruits."
The "enabling" (yuan) and "revealing" (liao) [factors] are but one aspect of Buddha-nature; this is precisely the cause.

Because Kāśyapa did not understand the Buddha’s answer—which is the true teaching where cause and effect are non-dual—he mistakenly regarded the fruits of wisdom and severance as possessing the nature of enabling and revealing.
These fruits of wisdom and severance involve both realization and vision; because the fruit is achieved through the cause and cultivated by means of the conditions, it is the fruit.
Because the cause is cultivated through decisive severance, the fruit is realized; thus, when evil dharmas within the causal stage are completely destroyed, this fruit is attained.
Since this fruit is achieved through the merit of distinct cultivation, is it not the case that there is cultivation in the cause and realization in the fruit?
If both cause and fruit are already likened to space, and space is a non-existent dharma, then the analogy is not equivalent; therefore, the Buddha-nature differs from space.
Because it is a metaphor for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), Kāśyapa asked: "If the Tathāgata, Buddha-nature, and *nirvāṇa* are existent, then space (*ākāśa*) should also be existent.
The Tathāgata verified the cause by means of the fruit, showing that all are like space; yet Kāśyapa verified the cause by comparing it to space as being different.
Depending on whether one follows the provisional or the ultimate teachings of the various schools, and whether one affirms or denies Buddha-nature, there arise various distinctions based upon this.

Furthermore, the sixth fascicle clarifies the Buddha-nature of the Tripitaka Teaching, while the ninth fascicle clarifies the Buddha-nature of the Separate Teaching and the thirty-two [marks].
This fascicle clarifies the Buddha-nature according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

This *śamatha-vipaśyanā* uses the three teachings to distinguish three sections of the sūtra text, all of which employ the metaphors of "mixed blood" and the "five flavors" to correspond respectively to ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddhas.
Why is it that the Buddha-nature within persons differs in its gradations across the three teachings? Since the three teachings are each distinct, the Buddha-nature should likewise be so.
There is a distinction here: according to the provisional teachings, Buddha-nature is not pervasive among insentient things, and thus it is termed "negation" (否).
Furthermore, in the twenty-seventh fascicle, it says: "If one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, one then sees Buddha-nature.

Cultivating the perfect Eightfold Noble Path is the "contemplating subject" (能觀), while the principle revealed by this seeing of Buddha-nature is the "object of contemplation" (所觀). This Buddha-nature pervades all phenomena.

Regarding the term "progress" (*jin*): the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* both maintain that the Eightfold Right Path does not pervade all phenomena within the Buddha-nature;

this is termed "regression" (*fu*). Conversely, even across various sutras—whether provisional or ultimate—it is held that the Eightfold Right Path is seen within the Buddha-nature as pervading all places; this is termed "progress. As for...
If one cultivates the Eightfold Right Path of the provisional teachings and views the Buddha-nature as not pervading all phenomena, is this not called "denial"?
What kind of Eightfold Right Path is being cultivated, and what kind of Buddha-nature?

Since one cannot clarify these matters regarding the Buddha-nature discussed within the provisional and real teachings—wherein there is both progress and denial—one uses the provisional *pratyaya-bodhi* (conditional awakening) and *upāya-bodhi* (means-awakening) to challenge the real *hetu-bodhi* (causal awakening). Therefore, it is said:

"This person does not know whether the Buddha-nature is advancing or not. The above passage generally summarizes the meaning of the Buddha-nature as elucidated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to refute his ignorance regarding whether the Buddha-nature is progressing or not, just as has been done here.
The guest asked: "For what reason do the provisional teachings not state that the two causes—conditions (*pratyaya*) and fulfillment (*paripūri*)—are universal?

I replied: "Sentient beings have, since beginningless time, conceived of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*). Because [the Buddha] taught in accordance with these conceptions, he did not yet speak of their universality. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the provisional is brought along with the real;

thus, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can be used as an analogy for the primary cause (*hetu*), but it cannot yet serve as an analogy for the conditions and fulfillment. If the teaching were exclusively provisional, then all three causes would be restricted."

Just as the initial hearing of the Correct [Teaching] by those at the stage of separate [vehicles] is likewise restricted to the *dharmatā* (store-nature) and the principle of nature, so it is for all [stages].

Therefore, when ordinary beings hear that insentient things have no basis, they become confused by what was shown and say, "The capacity to create belongs to [sentient beings]," thereby adhering to provisional teachings to establish a nature. They claim that which is created belongs to [insentient things], which is not the case.

Furthermore, throughout this one lifetime, many instances of the Sudden Teaching have already been revealed, such as in the *Avataṃsaka*, where the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, and Samantabhadra’s Universal Eye.

The three [bodies] are without distinction; the Great Assembly [Sūtra] teaches that all defiled and pure phenomena are mutually integrated. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* speaks of inconceivable pores containing all things;
the *Akṣayamati* and *Jālinīprabha* [parables] show that there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm. In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, all dharmas are mixed together as non-dual.

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the reality of the beginning and the end is identical to *nirvāṇa*. These [teachings] merely prevent the erroneous attachments of the degenerate age by distinguishing between the provisional and the real, the conditional and the fundamental, and by pointing toward the various directions.

If one clings to the real while being deluded regarding the provisional, one loses even the real; if one clings to the provisional while being deluded regarding the real, then one is deluded regarding both the provisional and the real.
Examining the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, it is seen that because they are still obscured by the mind, they remain ignorant of the Mahāyāna teachings.

The guest asked: "Is it only in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that the 'concurrent' (or 'inclusive') teaching is mentioned? I replied: "It is spoken of generally across the various sections; within the category of the 'Concurrent' section, there are indeed intermediate grades."
Whether it be the Real (shí) or the Expedient (quán), as in the case of Śāriputra’s challenge to Kāśyapa, they are distinguished merely for the sake of a specific capacity in the final age;
thus, both the Expedient and the Real are clarified together. If it were exclusively Expedient, it would be like the seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River;

if it were exclusively Real, it would be like the three dots, the two birds, the three types of compassion, the ten virtues, and so forth—all of which should be understood accordingly and cannot be described in detail. As it is said: "Form is permanent, form... [is impermanent].
How can it be said that [the teachings] do not encompass all things, both the primary and the secondary? Why then do you restrict the scope of emptiness?
These worldly people do not understand the provisional and the ultimate nature of the teachings.

This passage generally cites texts from throughout the one lifetime of the Buddha concerning the provisional and the ultimate to refute their ignorance regarding the provisional and ultimate nature of the teachings, following what was stated previously.
The text states that because the analogy of emptiness for the correct conditions and the aids to enlightenment (*pratyaya*) is still limited, a layman now asks:
"For what reason do the provisional teachings not state that the Buddha-nature of the two causes is pervasive even among insentient things? I replied:
"It is because sentient beings, since beginningless time, have clung to a self of provisional names and to a self of real dharmas consisting of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)."

Because these beings give rise to conceptual attachments based on the five aggregates as mere provisional names and thus become deluded regarding Buddha-nature, [the Buddha] points out the Buddha-nature of conditions (pratyaya) and causes (hetu) according to their own conceptualized aggregates and minds.

It was not yet appropriate to declare that it pervades even insentient things; this is because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* here speaks of the real "correct cause" (samyak-hetu) while still employing the provisional teachings on conditions and causes.
Therefore, it uses emptiness as a metaphor for the correct cause of the Real Teaching, but does not yet provide such a metaphor for [insentient matter].

The passage stating that in the provisional teaching, the conditions (yuan) and the fruition (liao) "bring along" the provisional while speaking of the real, indicates why the provisional teaching speaks only of the conditions and the fruition, whereas the real teaching speaks only of the true cause (zhengyin).
If the teaching were exclusively provisional, it would state that all three causes are restricted;

how could it be limited merely to the conditions and the fruition? For instance, when a person at the initial stage of the Separate Teaching hears of the true cause, that too is restricted—not to mention the other two.

The three causes are restricted to sentient beings; even such terms as "nature-store" (*dharmadhātu*), "nature-reason" (*prakṛti*), and "the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) are all applied to sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that "all are thus. Consequently, ordinary people at the level of the mundane ground certainly lack Buddha-nature regarding insentient things.
For those who demonstrate delusion based on delusion, one points out the object of their delusion and designates it as "the creating mind."
Within this, the existence of Buddha-nature is established based on the provisional teachings, stating that it is a derivative form (*upādāya-rūpa*) and not the Buddha-nature itself;
this is the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s inclusion of the provisional. Its true intent, however, lies in the reality of the Perfect and Sudden teaching.

This Perfect and Sudden teaching does not stop at the single era of the *Nirvāṇa*; within it, the principle that the perfect essence is all-pervasive has already been extensively revealed, even though in the interim...
There is a provisional, minor interpretation that intends [the teaching] to be sudden; thus, various sutras are cited, such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which states:
"Based on the middle, the correct appears; within the correct, the middle appears. The practices and vows of Samantabhadra are boundless; the realm of the universal eye is vast and great.
A single world-system enters all, and all likewise enter one. The same applies to mind, Buddha, and sentient beings."
The threefold non-differentiation—does this not indeed signify the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature?
In the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the ten realms of existence, both defiled and pure, are all mutually interfused; does this not indeed signify the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature?

In the "Inconceivable" chapter of the *Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra*, Mount Sumeru is contained within a mustard seed, and Mount Sumeru is contained within a mustard seed, as are the pores of the skin. Does this not indeed signify the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature?
To embrace this—is it not the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature? In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, the light of the jewel net’s radiance interpenetrates one another:
one encompasses all, and all encompass one; all phenomena are mutually fused, such that there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
Is this not the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature? In the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, all dharmas are merged as one.
This non-duality is surely the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena from beginning to end is exactly like this;
is it not the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature? As for the aforementioned Mahāyāna sūtras, they have already been [adapted] to the present conditions and capacities.
The meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature exists only within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as a safeguard against [future misconceptions].
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the periods of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma, there will be those whose faculties mistakenly cling to the provisional and the real;
it is necessary to clearly reveal the directions of the provisional and the real so that they do not remain in ignorance.

Therefore, among the three causes, the "direct cause" (zhengyin) is distinguished as specifically belonging to the real, while the "conditional cause" (yinyin) and "completed cause" (liaoyin) are distinguished as specifically belonging to the provisional; hence it is said that "the direct and the conditional are divided."
If one fails to understand the distinction between the provisional and the real, one will cling to each in opposition to the other.

If one clings to the "correct cause" of the real teaching while remaining deluded regarding the "conditional cause" and "conditional effect" of the provisional teaching, then by failing to realize that the provisional is itself the real, one loses even the real—how much more so would one fail to preserve the provisional?
Conversely, if one clings to the conditional cause and effect of the provisional teaching while remaining deluded regarding the correct cause of the real teaching, then as for the provisional...
In truth, both have perished. Even a rustic guest within the Sudden Teaching of *Nirvāṇa* is still confused regarding the meaning of the provisional and the real;

if you, my son, likewise fail to understand that all phenomena of the Lesser Vehicle arise from the mind, then how much more so for the profound meaning that the environments and inhabitants of the six realms are all created by the mind and that the retribution of karma is unfailing?
How could one possibly comprehend the myriad [teachings] of the Perfect and Real Great Teaching?

The Dharma is solely mind; there are no objects external to the mind, yet one is able to realize this. If there were even a single dharma arising from outside the mind, it could not be called "Mind-Only.
Since Buddha-nature is such that all dharmas are none other than Buddha-nature, how could insentient things be excluded?
This "wild guest" does not understand the four provisional teachings and the ultimate reality; therefore, he specifically disparages [the Mahayana] as being merely the most limited of the Tripitaka.

This is the ultimate point of censure. A rustic visitor, based on the preceding text, argues that because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* teaches the Real while retaining the Provisional, it is permissible to use emptiness as a metaphor for the Perfect [nature] and the Conditions and Causes [of Buddhahood].
However, this remains limited; therefore, he now asks: "In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, if it conforms to the Provisional, then all three causes must be provisional;
if it conforms to the Real, then all three causes must be real. How could it be merely a case of retaining the Provisional regarding the Conditions and Causes?"
Because it explains the true and direct cause, it is called *nirvāṇa*; how could this be merely an incidental or partial teaching? I replied: "There is indeed a reason for this.

If one speaks from a general perspective regarding the various sections (*bhu*), the four teachings (*catasraḥ śāsana-dharmāḥ*) are all included; while the provisional and partial are taught, the perfect and real (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) is also present.

Therefore, it is said that 'in terms of the sections, generally speaking, all are included as incidental. However, if one discusses each specific chapter (*varga*) within the sections, then within those chapters there may be the real."

Alternatively, there are those who speak of the provisional and the real as not being one, wherein the provisional and the real are presented together; and there are those who speak of them exclusively as either provisional or real.
If they are presented together, it is as in the *Kāśyapaparivarta*, where in response to Kāśyapa’s challenge, the discussion first challenges the real, as when it asks:
"How can the Buddha-nature of sentient beings be said to be 'like empty space'? and subsequently challenges the provisional.
If it is said that the Tathāgata, Buddha-nature, and Nirvāṇa exist, then space should also exist; this is taught specifically for the sake of a particular type of practitioner in the final age.

It is appropriate for the True Teaching (Shōkyō) to speak only of the Direct Cause (Jūin), and appropriate for the Provisional Teaching (Gengi) to speak only of the Contributory and Developmental Causes (En-in and Ryō-in).
This [present teaching], however, speaks by combining both the provisional and the real. If it were exclusively provisional...
The "seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River" uses fish as a metaphor. Although there are only four types of fish, they are categorized into seven by pairing them;
these are used as metaphors for humans, hence the designation of "seven kinds. These are: those who are constantly submerged, those who emerge briefly, and those who remain after emerging.

Those who are constantly submerged are like large fish, serving as a metaphor for *icchantikas* and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who possess only minor roots of goodness. Once they have emerged, they remain [on the surface].

The simile of the *cimi* fish illustrates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and those who have attained the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). After emerging, they observe in each direction;

having observed, they move; having moved, they stop again. The simile of the *xi* fish illustrates the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), as well as the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) reaching the other shore.
The simile of the divine tortoise, which moves both on land and in water, illustrates the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha.

The intent of the sutra uses the Nirvana of the Shared Teaching as a metaphor for a river, yet it refutes this from the perspective of the Distinct Teaching by stating that these seven types of people are all unable to cultivate their bodies, precepts, minds, and wisdom; thus, one knows they are provisional.

If they were exclusively real, it would be as explained in the "Chapter on Sighing" (Saṃnipāta-parivarta), where the three dots of the letter *i* serve as a metaphor for the perfect fusion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), as clarified in the "Bird Metaphor."
The two birds flying together serves as a metaphor for the twofold function of perfect interfusion, as clarified in the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (Brahmacarya-parivarta).
The three types of non-referential compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) of sentient beings according to the Perfect Teaching are clarified in the "Chapter on King Virtue" (Guṇarāja-parivarta).
Since the true meanings in the aforementioned chapters are exceedingly numerous, they are designated as "others. [This refers to] that which is contained within other chapters.
The true meaning can be understood by analogy with this and need not be described in detail; this refers generally to the "three causes" of the Real Teaching (*śāsanadharma*).
Furthermore, it specifically points to the statement in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* (Cienru pin): "When form is extinguished, one obtains eternal form.
How could this not include all forms of both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-pratisthā*)? This is the essence of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
This is because the substance of Buddha-nature pervades both sentient and insentient beings, just as empty space pervades all places.
Why, then, is Buddha-nature restricted solely to the bodies of sentient beings? Why is empty space constrained and limited?
If one uses provisional conditions to challenge the ultimate reality, it is because these people of the world do not understand the teachings.

This discussion of the provisional and the real is based on the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime teaching to refute those "rustic guests" who do not understand the provisional and real aspects of the teachings;

for it was because Jingxi deeply grasped the intent of the provisional and real throughout the entire dispensation that he was able to refute those rustic guests who did not know whether or not they possessed Buddha-nature.

Just as those of the Two Vehicles hear of the Great [Vehicle] everywhere yet only reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* before believing their own nature and repenting that they have come here with wealth that was not theirs—does this not mean they did not know their father’s nature?
Only after hearing the revelation of the provisional (*upāya*) do they say they have the capacity for transformation through the mouth and birth by transformation;
thus, even in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is still fear that a portion of sentient beings in the future will not believe in their own [Buddha-nature].

If the body possesses the nature of the Tathāgata, and it is said that icchantikas will never sever [their roots] in the future, yet this is shown to make them know that [the nature] exists and is not severed—
how could there be no sudden [attainment] at all within the various texts of this school?

This uses the circumstances of those with the capacity [to understand] while the Buddha was in the world as an analogy for the capacity of future beings, clarifying the intent behind the teaching of the provisional within the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra to reveal the ultimate reality.
For example, when people of the Two Vehicles were within the *Avataṃsaka*, they did not believe in the Great [Vehicle] when it was presented to them;

when they were within the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā), they were still attached to the small fruits despite being rebuked by the Great. Then, in the *Prajñā* teachings, the instruction was transferred to them.
Those of the two vehicles who possessed wealth considered themselves correct, claiming that the Bodhisattva dharma-gate was not their own possession;

it was only upon hearing the threefold revelation in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—wherein the five Buddhas’ assemblies were shown to be identical—that they finally believed their own bodies possessed the Tathāgata-nature.

Thus, the passage from the sūtra stating, "I have come here to repent," refers to the text of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding. This is based on the capacity of those of the Small Vehicle regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, [who previously lacked such realization].

Because one has received the great transformation, it is said that one regrets having come, like clouds dispersing at their end. When the impoverished son sees his father’s great power and majesty, he immediately conceives fear and regrets having come here;
thinking "this wealth is not mine," it is as described in the section on receiving and returning items:

having received and taken inventory of the various goods, gold, silver, precious jewels, and so forth, yet lacking the slightest intention to take even a single meal, only then does it say, "it arises from the mouth."

Regarding those born by transformation, as stated in the Parable Chapter: "Only today do I know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, and having obtained a share of the Buddha-Dharma.

If even those with present-day faculties must wait until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to believe in their inherent nature, how much more so must those future beings of a certain class—whose obstructions are heavy and whose faculties are dull—after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa? They certainly will.
Is it possible to cause them to have confidence that they themselves possess the Buddha-nature?
Therefore, even in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is still concern that a portion of sentient beings in the future will not believe that they themselves possess the Tathāgata-nature;
not only do they fail to believe that the Buddha-nature exists within their own bodies, but they also claim that icchantikas, because of their extreme evil, shall never possess it in future lives.
Because the Buddha-nature is intended for such a capacity, it is pointed out within the minds of sentient beings to cause them to know that it exists.
Kāśyapa, knowing this capacity, raised his doubt precisely because he understood that there would be sentient beings in the future who would not believe in the existence of the nature.
Thus, the Tathāgata, relying on provisional teachings, spoke of Buddha-nature as being restricted to sentient beings alone, saying, "It does not exist in non-sentient things."
"Nature" refers to walls, tiles, and rubble; this reveals that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature with the intention of employing provisional means (*upāya*).
Within this *Nirvāṇa* section, the provisional gate is indicated incidentally, while the primary focus lies in the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) teaching.
Furthermore, within this single dispensation (*śāsana*), the Sudden has already been extensively revealed; therefore, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings within this section is like empty space.
The passages on emptiness, the three dots, the two birds, and so forth—all of these are sudden teachings within the same division (nikāya). Thus, one asks:

"Is it that there are no sudden teachings at all within this division? If this is the case, then the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the fundamental and the manifested aspects of the Perfect-Sudden teaching for the sake of future capacities, because these two sūtras are both of the "ghee" (paramārtha) stage.

Regarding the single work *Jīnbī* (The Golden Scalpel), when I read it in the past, it was as obscure as wandering at night, and I knew not where it was headed.
Recently, the Venerable Dákōng happened to obtain a copy of the *Shìwén* (Explanatory Text)—that is, a commentary on the *Jīnbī*. Consequently, I borrowed it and read it.
After reading it four or five times, as if he had understood one or two points, what was previously obscure has now become entirely clear.
How can his joy and exultation be described? My only regret is that the woodblocks are kept in another province, making them difficult for the public to obtain;

thus, I have enlisted the help of my fellow practitioners to entrust this work to woodblocks so that it may be widely disseminated. May all who see or hear it realize that delusive defilements are themselves Buddha-nature, and attain immediate understanding.
If all worldly phenomena were eternally constant, then the Patriarch’s discourse would have been nothing but a sleep-talker;
could it have awakened the slumbering saliva of all sentient beings across the great earth? This record is briefly inscribed upon the completion of the construction, merely to note its origins.
On the Buddha’s Birthday in the first month of summer in the first year of the Tianqi era, the monk Yuanbing of Dongyan Jingge respectfully records this.

The Tiantai śramaṇa Shiju explains that for later students, the newly established [doctrines] are not yet perfected;

though they seek to establish a comprehensive and non-deficient nature, they are merely hindered by the obstruction of principle. Therefore, within the nature itself, he points out its pervasive essence to incidentally refute the partial indication of "pure *tathatā*," for even this fails to preserve the small-scale reality of Buddha-nature.

*An* (安). (Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on the concept of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and critiques those who, while seeking a universal nature, fall into conceptual obstructions or misrepresent the true meaning of pure *tathatā*.)

Because they do not understand the fundamental tenets of our school’s established doctrine regarding the existence or non-existence of insentient things within the emptiness of his absence, those who have realized the essence of Mind-Only must consider whether there is any difference [between them and us].

If Mind-Only were not established, all the Great Teachings would be entirely useless; if one does not allow that the mind possesses the principle of perfect immediacy (*endon*), then faith becomes a mere empty gesture.
If one harbors further doubts regarding the existence or non-existence of what is "mind-only," then one is doubting the existence or non-existence of one's own mind.

Therefore, know that a single speck of dust and a single moment of mind are the very nature of the mind of all sentient beings and Buddhas; how could they alone be the existence or non-existence of one's own mind?
This is because they are co-created, co-transformed, share the same objective realm, and share the same transformative phenomena.

Now, our school establishes the principle that the Buddha-nature is perfectly interfused, all-pervasive, and inherently complete within the mind, based upon the two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, we clarify the true intent behind establishing these tenets so that they may lead back to the Single Reality (*ekayāna*).

We take the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the primary basis for revealing the provisional to manifest the real and clarifying the meaning of eternal abiding for the sake of those with karmic conditions in the present age; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* serves as...
Regarding the future opportunities for discourse on the eternally abiding Buddha-nature, these two sutras are distinguished from one another;
thus, the *Mohe zhiguan* establishes the practice of perfect interfusion based upon these two sutras. Therefore, the *Yili* states:

"While various passages are cited at length to encompass the entire body of teachings throughout the One Vehicle, the primary intent of their textual substance ultimately returns to these two sutras. Now, Jingxi likewise emulates the *Zhiguan*.
The purpose of establishing the principle of the perfectly interfused Buddha-nature differs from the error of the "wild guests" who claim that insentient things lack Buddha-nature;

thus it is said, "not being afflicted by the nature. To be "afflicted" means to be hindered. However, while one may be afflicted, if one does not understand the principle of Buddha-nature, this true reality will remain obstructed and unpenetrated.
Consequently, right view becomes restricted to the Buddha-nature of sentient beings alone, failing to encompass all things universally.

Because insentient things lack [sentience], it is now demonstrated that within the essence of the deluded and defiled minds of sentient beings, the originally existent *tathāgatagarbha* (the true cause of Buddhahood) is present;
this is not something that exists internally or externally, pervading empty space.

One who can understand this meaning will spontaneously find no separation from insentient things, thereby establishing that insentient things possess Buddha-nature. Therefore, it is said: "Within the nature, the pervasive essence is pointed out."
This is precisely the fact that the essence of the true cause of sentient beings is all-pervasive. Regarding the refutation of those who point exclusively to pure *tathatā*:

"exclusively" (*páng*) is said in contrast to "the true" (*zhèng*). The reason for pointing out here that the essence is all-pervasive is precisely to reveal the meaning that delusive defilements are themselves Buddha-nature;
this resides here and not elsewhere. For other schools point exclusively to sentient beings [as the locus of Buddha-nature].

There is a nature of purity that is restricted solely to sentient beings and does not pervade insentient things; this is because they have lost the essential principle that the substance [of reality] is comprised of Mind-Only.
Therefore, we now establish the doctrine of perfect interfusion to prevent such erroneous attachments. The term "partial" (or "one-sided") contains two meanings:
first, it refers to being deluded regarding the causal principle while focusing on the phenomenal fruit of affliction—meaning that within the causal state of sentient beings, there is only...
Regarding its nature yet lacking its phenomena, one does not realize that the fruit-ground (the state of Buddhahood) is the fusion of the environment and its inhabitants;
this is because the fundamental principle of all sentient beings is inherently complete. Second, as for the fusion of Buddha-nature, how could it exclude the insentient?

To claim that the sentient possess nature while the insentient do not is a misconception. Not only is their understanding thus, but even when establishing their practice, they directly contemplate [this truth].

Since it is originally without characteristics, what further cultivation could there be? To "see the Muni" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*.

If you maintain that the *dharmatā* is called "non-awakening" (unconsciousness) and exists exclusively in insentient things, differing from Buddha-nature, for what reason do you now [speak] regarding the *dharma*...?
The nature is fundamentally pure, signless, and beyond cultivation; can one see the Muni?

The fourfold wisdom of reality states that "signlessness" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), for it is free from the signs of defilement and obstruction; thus, the true Buddha-body is signless and is indeed the Dharma-body.

The Dharma-body pervades all places, and the two bodies (the Reward-body and Transformation-body) are eternally present within it. These three are fused and identical, never having been separated for even a moment. If one perceives this Dharma...
How could the body possibly allow for a deviation from these two? The preceding two bodies are likewise so; the text merely speaks of them separately.

Since you have understood that the essence of the True Buddha resides within all phenomena, you should not, according to your own feelings, differentiate between the sentient and the insentient, or between Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature.
I ask you to reflect upon this. Furthermore, I shall continue to challenge you regarding your adherence to or rejection of the teachings, as if addressing a rustic guest.
The deluded view that insentient things possess only the name "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) and should not be established as having the name "buddha-nature" (buddhadhātu) is incorrect;

therefore, we now explain it according to reality by asserting that dharma-nature is itself buddha-nature. This is precisely the progression toward the buddha-nature of the definitive teaching (nītārtha) as expounded in the aforementioned Great Sūtra.
If one does not permit the establishment of the name "buddha-nature" with respect to insentient things, this would contradict what was previously stated.
Speaking with such qualifications regarding the existence or non-existence of Buddha-nature, I intend for the simple-minded guest to surely believe that even insentient things possess Buddha-nature.
Therefore, True Suchness following conditions is precisely Buddha-nature following conditions; the single character "Buddha" (佛) is itself the Dharma-Buddha (法佛). Thus, the Dharma...
Because the Buddha and *tathatā* (suchness) are one in essence and differ only in name, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, fascicle 1, states:

"Buddha-nature is precisely the *tathatā* manifested by the twofold emptiness of person and phenomena. One should know that *tathatā* is simply another name for Buddha-nature. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:
"Both 'sentient beings' and 'non-sentient beings' lack any true reality; thus, the actual meaning of the nature of all phenomena is that neither exists."
To say that sentient beings are not sentient beings—does this not mean that both the animate and the inanimate follow conditions while remaining simultaneously unchanging?

Therefore, both are non-existent; thus, within the *dharmadhātu* and the *bhūtakoṭi*, all things are likewise so. One should know that the name "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) does not apply exclusively to the *tathatā* (suchness) found among insentient things.
This is because worldly people are collectively deluded regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), mistaking differences in name for differences in essence.
This is because they are one and the same.
Since it has been shown that the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is itself the buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), it is understood that the buddha-nature is not restricted solely to sentient beings.
Not only is the dharma-nature the buddha-nature, but the suchness (*tathatā*) that accords with conditions is also the buddha-nature; these are merely different names for the same reality.

To refute that view which posits a distinction between True Suchness (*tathatā*) following conditions throughout both sentient and insentient beings, and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) or Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), this passage now provides a comprehensive synthesis;
thus it says: "True Suchness following conditions is precisely Buddha-nature following conditions. The single character "Buddha" (*buddha*) refers to the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*).
"Dharma" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), for the Dharma-body is the principle through which True Suchness is realized; thus, the name [Buddha] accords with what was stated above.
This is because the meaning of the established thesis concerns the pervasive nature of the true cause (*hetu*).

Other schools merely know that the *dharmakāya* is pervasive, but do not realize that *tathatā* following conditions (*pratyaya*) is precisely the pervasive nature of the *dharmakāya*, and that the pervasive nature of the *dharmakāya* is the pervasive nature of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Therefore, the Master of the Commentary (*Ji-zhu*) unifies the terminology by identifying the nature of the Dharma-Buddha with the name "Tathatā," bringing them onto a single track. Buddha-nature.

This treatise consists of four fascicles and was composed by Vasubandhu. He states that Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is precisely the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested through the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena.

Therefore, I now cite this to harmonize [the various teachings], as their names differ while their essence is the same. The two kinds of emptiness of persons and phenomena are the contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*) that acts as the manifestor;
*tathatā* and Buddha-nature are the rational essence (*dharmatā*) manifested thereby. Thus, the concluding synthesis states: "One should know that *tathatā*..."
This is simply another name for Buddha-nature. Next, citing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is shown that the dharma-nature accords with conditions to manifest as suchness;
thus, its essence is identical whether it pertains to sentient beings or non-sentient beings. That is to say, both the animate and the inanimate accord with conditions.

Although both accord with conditions, they remain unchanging in their very place. If one realizes this immutability, the appearances of "accruing with conditions" naturally vanish. Therefore, it is said:
Because they are all equally unchanging, none of them possess [independent] existence; thus, the following serves as a general principle for the names previously listed, such as the *dharmadhātu*.
These names differ from the term "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) in expression but are identical in essence, all possessing the meaning of being both conforming to conditions and remaining unchanging.
They encompass both the sentient and the insentient without distinction. Therefore, one knows that the name "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) does not apply exclusively to the insentient.

In this world, people are deluded regarding the characteristics of dharmas; because they take the essence to be one while the names differ, they divide *tathatā* into two schools, causing the great principles of Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature to fall into discord.

Nevertheless, although they are identical in essence, there are minor distinctions. Generally, those names that include the term "nature" (*xing*) mostly pertain to ordinary beings or the principle (*li*), such as "Buddha-nature," "principle-nature," "true nature," "storehouse-nature," or "actual nature.

Those names that lack the term "nature" mostly apply universally to both ordinary beings and sages, as well as to cause and effect, and phenomenon and principle, such as "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) and "actual mark" (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as terms like "samādhi," "dhāraṇī," and "pāramitā."

Since equality pertains solely to the fruit, as for why the cause is termed "Buddha-nature" (buddhadhātu): although sentient beings have not yet actually attained Buddhahood, they realize the principle and verify the truth;
by opening the treasury, they demonstrate that afflictions and birth-and-death are the Buddha’s nature of equality, instructing them to practice this, which is thus called "Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, within the various teachings, these various names are established interchangeably.

The above demonstrates that throughout the various sūtras and śāstras, all names used to clarify the *dharmadhātu* and other such concepts are instances where the names differ while the essence remains the same;

yet, within this sameness, there are not a few distinctions. This is because among these various names, there are those designated as "having nature" (*sasvabhāva*) and those designated as "without nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).

For example, the five names for *buddhadhātu* mostly refer to ordinary beings, whereas the term "principle" (*li*) mostly refers to the state of reality. The phrase "mostly" is used here because it follows the predominant or stronger sense of each term.

To speak of "many" necessarily implies a contrast with "few," yet there is also a general sense in which this applies. If one speaks of the "Dharmadhātu" and so forth as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), this term "many" generally encompasses both ordinary beings and sages, as well as cause and effect, and phenomena and principle.

This is because *dhāraṇī* refers to the secret and essential methods of total retention attained by those who have reached fruition, while *pāramitā* refers to the ultimate *nirvāṇa*, the far shore to which those who have reached fruition have gone. As it is said:

Terms such as "samādhi" and so forth apply exclusively to the stage after fruition; the distinct designation of the cause as "Buddha-nature" (buddhatā) is because sentient beings have not yet actually attained Buddhahood.
Through the realization of principle and the verification of truth, the treasury is opened.

Since afflictions and birth-and-death are adventitious evils (pratipakṣa-doṣa), they have arisen from the very nature [of reality] since beginningless time; therefore, these adventitious evil natures are now designated as "intrinsically evil" (prakṛti-pāpa).
Because it is taught so as to lead one to practice in accordance with the nature, it is called "Buddha-nature," "the nature of reality" (*dharmatā*), and so forth;

thus, various names are established interchangeably across the teachings. As previously mentioned, regarding the names for the causal nature and the resultant virtue found within the various teachings, these various names are also established interchangeably and are not unilaterally fixed.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the term "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*) is frequently used because the Buddha is one who has realized the fruit, and it is said that all sentient beings possess the nature of such a person of the fruit;
therefore, this term is emphasized. Because worldly people are deluded and do not proceed toward the fruit, they fail to realize that its essence is pervasive.
Furthermore, it is said to be "pervasive" because the essence of the mind-nature is pervasive even within afflictions; thus, it is called "the pervasiveness of Buddha-nature."
Therefore, know that the failure to realize the pervasiveness of Buddha-nature is precisely due to not knowing the pervasiveness of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*).

How could the term "Mind-Only" refer solely to the True Mind? My son, if you do not yet understand the pervasiveness of the mind of afflictions, how can you possibly comprehend the pervasiveness of the form (*rūpa*) of birth-and-death?
Why is form pervasive? Because form is itself the mind.
However, the essence of the Dharma-gate of great universal characteristics is fundamentally without high or low;

yet, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the character "Buddha" (*buddha*) is specifically added above the character "nature" (*prakṛti*). This is because sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses;

for this reason, it is specifically proclaimed that this name is established by relying on the fruit to illustrate the cause, stating that all sentient beings possess the nature of the person who has realized the fruit. There is no [other] nature.

There is no distinction between these two; the desire for them to reform their delusions and turn toward enlightenment—from cause to fruit—is that they may equally partake in the enjoyment of the Buddha.
Therefore, this is stated specifically. This interpenetration of the environment and the inhabitants within the state of fruition is fully possessed by the fundamental nature of all sentient beings.

Yet, worldly people are deluded regarding this and do not follow the principle of the interpenetration of the environment and inhabitants at the level of fruition, but merely speak of "sentient beings" (sattvas).

If there is Buddha-nature in sentient beings and no Buddha-nature in insentient things, yet one knows that on the level of the fruit, the environment and its inhabitants are interfused, and that this is fundamentally inherent in the causal mind—how could one then differentiate between sentient and insentient, thereby losing the principle of the pervasiveness of the essence? Furthermore, it says:

"As for 'pervasiveness,' the following explains the meaning of pervasiveness according to the sutra to refute such doubts; the reason it is pervasive is precisely because of the afflictions of sentient beings."
Since the essence of the mind-nature is all-pervasive, it is said that Buddha-nature is all-pervasive. As stated above, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space;
because from time immemorial the entirety of nature has given rise to cultivation, it is termed the "class of afflictions.
Thus, at the very moment of arising, these seeds transform entirely into cultivation. Therefore, what is now pointed out as cultivation is itself nature for all sentient beings.
Because this nature exists, this is the Tathāgata-gotra; it is primordially pervasive, and thus is called the "pervasiveness of Buddha-nature.
