Therefore, one should know that those who fail to recognize the pervasiveness of Buddha-nature do so because they point exclusively to pure *tathatā* (suchness), without realizing that the pervasiveness of the nature of afflictions is itself the pervasiveness of Buddha-nature.
What is called "mind-only" refers precisely to the mind of afflictions; it is not merely—

If one does not recognize that the essence of Buddha-nature is all-pervasive, one also loses the meaning of "mind-only. Therefore, when practicing contemplation, one directly contemplates the true mind.
If you, my son, do not yet know that the mind of afflictions is pervasive, how can you know that the form of birth-and-death is pervasive?

Because form is identical to mind, the environment and its inhabitants are of one suchness within a single thought-moment; thus, the essence of the *samyak-hetu* (correct cause) of sentient beings is all-pervasive.
The Fourth Clarification states: "If one believes that all forms are identical to mind, then it is established that insentient things possess the principle of Buddha-nature.
As for 'the forms of birth-and-death,' these refer to the forms of both the segmented and the transformational [births]; thus they are called 'birth-and-death.
If categorized according to the ten realms, they belong to the forms of the nine realms; because ignorance has not yet been exhausted, they are called 'birth-and-death.'"
My ancestor said that "quiescence" refers to the extinction of the five abodes and the two deaths.

Why is this? The environment (the *niśraya-vipāka*) is collectively created, while the physical body (the *adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*) is individually created; how could one believe in the collective pervasiveness [of the mind] while disbelieving its individual pervasiveness?
Since both the creator and the created are merely mind, and the essence of mind cannot be confined to any specific location, it is for this reason that the Buddhas of the ten directions...
All lands possess the seeds of the rational mind within the principle of the nature of beings; this nature is likened to space, as fully described in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Furthermore, it is evident that failing to understand the names, essences, and similarities or differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings is a great affliction for those who study the Buddhist doctrine.
Thus, Śāriputra said: "We have likewise entered the same dharma-nature and have also attained liberation," and so forth.
At this point, the inquiry is raised to explain the preceding meaning that form is universally fused within the very mind. Why is it that form is universal?

It is precisely because both the "support" (*āśraya*) and the "primary retribution" (*mukhya-vipāka*) are matters produced through transformation according to conditions. The mountains, rivers, and lands are the support-retribution;
the five aggregates and material qualities are the primary retribution. Both are moved by common karma, appearing as sand, pebbles, thorns, and brambles.
It is produced through both collective and individual karma; that which is induced by different karmas results in distinct forms, whether vast or minute.

Although the production is both collective and individual, since they both originate from a single source, when there are two, both are two, and when there is one, both are one. These two are mutually identical because the mind is all-pervasive; therefore, form is also all-pervasive.
How could one believe in collective pervasion while disbelieving in individual pervasion? Such a statement is not intended as a rebuke to a rustic visitor; rather, it is the intended meaning.

This means that the primary retribution (vipāka) created by sentient beings individually and the secondary retribution (niśraya) created by them collectively both exist as the entire body, produced through transformation according to conditions (*pratyaya*).
Within this process of transformation according to conditions, there is merely a distinction between the subjective and objective aspects of mind and matter (*citta-rūpa*).

Now, to clarify that matter is all-pervasive, we discuss the equality of the fundamental reality (*dharmatā*) wherein matter and mind are non-dual; this reveals the pervasiveness of the wondrous realm. If one has faith...
Since the essential nature of form that accords with conditions is fundamentally all-pervasive, how could there not be a mind that accords with conditions whose essence is likewise pervasive?

This is the intended meaning of this exposition. Although this provisional [reliance] and the ultimate reality are differentiated as subject and object from the perspective of following conditions, since both are solely the substance of the mind and the substance of the mind is all-pervasive, it extends horizontally and exhausts vertically; how, then, can it be restricted by spatial location?
Is there existence or non-existence? When worldly people confine Vairocana within the physical aggregates, he exists within a specific location;

this is why the Buddha-lands of the ten directions all possess the rational nature and mental seeds of sentient beings. What are called "rational nature and mental seeds" originally comprise the three paths;
when referring to cultivation, they are identical to nature—that is, the three Buddha-natures—because they have never [been separated from it].

The application of the resolve for enlightenment is termed the "nature" (*dhātu*); "seed" (*gotra*) signifies that which is capable of producing. The host of afflictions is the "Tathāgata-seed," meaning it is inherently present from the beginning.

These three types of natures are fundamentally all-pervasive; they are the essence of the present mind, capable of producing all things—both the environment and its inhabitants (*sāśraya-dharmakāya*).
Thus, a sutra says: "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external; it is like space."

There are obstructions because their nature is likened to emptiness, as fully explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Furthermore, the "returning to the source" of Buddha-nature serves to reject the heterodox and manifest the orthodox;

this is also why it is used to indirectly censure worldly people and rustic folk. Thus we know that the following section concludes with a reprimand based on the identity or difference between names and essence.
In the various teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, names may be the same while the essence differs, or the name may differ while the essence remains the same.
While the names "Dharmatā," "Liberation," and so forth may be shared across the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, their referents are eternally distinct;

likewise, while names such as "Mahāyāna," "Buddha-nature," and "Tathatā" differ, their essence is identical. For those who study and explain the teachings, failing to comprehend this is a grave affliction.
Therefore, I cite the *Lotus Sūtra* and other texts to prove that we all equally enter into Dharmatā.
Thus, although the names "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha*) and "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) are the same, their meanings differ; liberation is likewise so.

You initially did not comprehend my intended meaning, and therefore you were startled and alarmed upon hearing it. To explain my own reasoning for your sake, you should understand that it is appropriate for your mind to become clear.
Therefore, know that worldly people are limited in their view of me, Vairocana; they perceive only within the physical aggregates and directly claim that all phenomena are non-existent.
Regarding "sentient beings," there are two ways in which this is superior [to other views]. First, it is superior to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Even the non-Buddhists claim that the self is large and form is small, and that the self pervades empty space; furthermore, they still reckon that [the world] is composed of various atoms (*paramāṇu*), rather than simply asserting that there are no sentient beings.
Second, it is superior to the Hīnayāna. Even the Hīnayāna claims that [existence] is created by the power of karma and that these creations pervade the three realms. Furthermore...
Even those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) know that all phenomena are impermanent; they do not merely speak of them as being insentient.

Furthermore, there are two types [of practitioners] who are inferior to those of the Shared Vehicle (Sādhāraṇayāna). Those of the Shared Vehicle still know that the mind creates illusions which pervade the three realms, and they also know that the essential nature of all phenomena is itself the Truth.
Since this is the case for the Successive Vehicle (Anupūrvayāna), it is not something you can even conceive of. Having heard this, you should also come to have a slight understanding.
Regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Dharma, the presence or absence of Buddha-nature, and the progression or regression [of sentient beings]:

when you first heard that insentient things possess Buddha-nature, your mind was bewildered and your heart was startled; this was because you had not yet fully grasped the essential meaning of the principles I established.

Now that I have explained for you, starting from the Great Sūtras regarding the progression and regression, the provisional and the ultimate, and concluding with the [distinction between] names and reality...
Having already explained in detail the nuances of the identity and difference of the essence, it is now resolved as clearly as ice melting;

yet those in the world who confine the *dharmakāya* Buddha-nature within the material aggregates of sentient beings and simply claim that all phenomena are insentient not only misunderstand the principle of the Great Teaching regarding the pervasive nature of the essence, but they fall short even of the heterodox, external, and limited schools.
For example: [The passage continues with a comparison between the Mahayana view of the pervasive Buddha-nature and the limited views of other traditions.]

There are two types of non-Buddhists: first, those who conceive of a self-soul (*ātman*) that is either larger than the body while the body is smaller, or as being all-pervasive such that there is no part of space that is not this self;
second, those who conceive of the body as being composed of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Although their specific conceptions differ, they all maintain the notion that the self pervades insentient matter and other forms of physicality; it is not merely the case that they claim the self exists within sentient beings alone.
Furthermore, as in the two truths of the Hīnayāna: first, the power of karma constructs the triple world;

since karma arises from the mind, it is "created by the mind," which is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) in its substantial sense. Moreover, knowing that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is impermanent is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
These are explained according to the two truths of the Hīnayāna, and they do not simply state that insentient things [lack consciousness], as is common [in other schools].
The "Vehicle" (yāna) refers to the two types within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*): first, it explains that the mind which creates [phenomena] is like an illusion or a transformation;

since illusion pervades the three realms, there is nothing it does not encompass—this is the conventional truth of illusory existence. Furthermore, knowing that the essential nature of all phenomena is emptiness in its very substance is the ultimate truth.
Since this is spoken in terms of the two truths shared by both vehicles, how could it refer merely to insentient things? If...

The gradual vehicles and the distinct teachings cannot fathom this, for they expound the principle that the One True Mind universally creates all phenomena; since their mental and physical natures do not pervade [all things], they are not capable of such realization.

Furthermore, those who have heard this should understand—through the many rounds of guidance and instruction provided above—that they must gain a basic knowledge of the provisional and real aspects of the teachings, and the meaning of whether Buddha-nature is present or absent. This repeated striking of the point is intended to bring about their awakening and understanding.
The guest said, "You have skillfully distinguished the reality and dispelled my heavy doubts.

Yet, while you state that all dharmas are by nature the true cause, you also say that within the Middle Way there are three types of causes, and that these causes pervade the fruit and the fruit pervades the cause; furthermore, you say that a single speck of dust or a single mind is immediately the mind-nature and essence of all sentient beings and Buddhas.
My understanding remains undecided. I replied, "This is truly because from the past you have not been able to comprehensively grasp the relationship between cause and effect."
When one observes oneself and others, as well as the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, through the correct contemplation of the dependent and the primary [realms],
yet remains unacquainted with the general purport of the various teachings and fails to understand the meaning of the Buddha’s discourse on the fruition-virtues (*phala-guṇa*),

nor grasps the reason for the mutual interpenetration manifested by the Buddha— desiring further to guide your disposition, I shall ask you forty-six questions; if you can understand my [intentions]...

A single question causes all obstructions to vanish of their own accord; the Dharma-realm is harmoniously integrated, and with vast clarity, one gains a comprehensive vision that penetrates the Dharma-realm.
One realizes that within a single thought-moment, the Buddhas and sentient beings, the environment and its inhabitants, are fully present without deficiency, even down to a single speck of dust.

Ever since the "Wild Guest" raised objections based on the Mahāyāna sūtras regarding the insentient being devoid of nature, commentators have provided judgments on the provisional and ultimate aspects of *nirvāṇa*, the meaning of whether *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) is present or absent, and have simultaneously demonstrated the principles of "mind-only" and "form-only.

They have further elucidated the meaning that the nature of afflictions is pervasive and that cultivation is universal; yet, as these points were treated section by section with increasing looseness, it was only now that the nature of tiles and stones was finally understood.
The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is provisional, while the pervasive essence of space is real; therefore, it is said that the benevolent one skillfully distinguishes them.

This truly destroys heavy doubts regarding the provisional and shatters biased doubts regarding the real. Although this meaning has been understood, one has not yet fully realized it as described above:

that the seed is pervasive, the cultivation is pervasive, and the fruit is pervasive—such that within a single speck of dust and a single thought, there is the mind of all sentient beings and Buddhas.

If the nature and other aspects were not fully explained by extensively demonstrating the principle of the perfect fulfillment of the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*) according to this single school, the subtle excellence of the perfect understanding could never have been exhausted;
therefore, using the pretext that "sentiment remains undecided," the subsequent text is introduced.
Furthermore, the single character "complete" (*ju*) more clearly reveals how our school refutes the hundred schools and transcends them all.

The various commentators clarify within their contemplation of the mind that ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness, and that form and fragrance are extinguished and purified, even to the point of not exceeding a single thought-moment of an ordinary person;
this is because [the Buddha-nature] is fully possessed [by all]. That it pervades the insentient is precisely this.

Formerly, it was reckoned that Buddha-nature was restricted solely to sentient beings; now, having received this instruction, we know that the nature of the true cause pervades both the sentient and the insentient.

For this reason, it is said that one must believe that all dharmas possess the nature of the true cause (*zhengyin*). Yet, there remains doubt as to whether the nature of the conditions (*yuanxing*) and the nature of the completion (*liaoxing*) are pervasive throughout the cultivation, the fruit, and the entirety of existence.
This refers to the preceding text: if the sudden teaching were to speak of reality, the three kinds of threefold principles would fundamentally be pervasive;

by realizing the nature, cultivation is perfected, and the three aspects of cultivation are likewise pervasive. Although the "fruit" is not explicitly mentioned, since it is stated that cultivation is pervasive, the fruit must necessarily be established accordingly.
The fruits and fruits are contained therein; this is why it was previously stated that in all Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there exist the principle-nature and mind-seeds of sentient beings.

When speaking of the three causal seeds, these are precisely the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). As for the pervasiveness of cultivation, both [the nature and the mind] are cultivated, and each likewise possesses the three.
As for the pervasiveness of the fruit, when one Buddha attains enlightenment, the entire Dharma-realm is none other than this Buddha.

This refers to the environment and the inhabitants [the *niśraya* and *sambhoga*]; therefore, it is said that when the three thousand realms are perfected as the fruit, they all partake in permanence and bliss.

Although what was previously stated regarding the pervasiveness of the *dharmadhātu-nature* (the *zhengyin*) has already been roughly understood, doubts still remain unresolved concerning the statement that "all three causes are equally pervasive. I replied:

"The following passage means that because people have not yet attained a thorough understanding of the principle that the teachings and contemplation are perfectly complete, it is now explained from the perspective of contemplation (*guan*). This has been so since ancient times."

If one does not skillfully grasp the principle that cause and effect, self and other, and the environment and its inhabitants are non-different from one's own mind—the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—then one will remain ignorant of the meanings of the "all-pervading seeds" and so forth.

This is the fault of failing to skillfully contemplate the mind as it is endowed with these qualities. As the text says: "Cause and effect, self and other, the environment and its inhabitants—these three pairs, when considered collectively," etc.

To explain the principle of "the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" separately: because one does not universally encompass cause and effect to contemplate one's own mind, one fails to understand that the seeds are universal.
Because one does not universally cultivate the universal cause to observe the universal fruit, one fails to understand that the unwholesome is universal.

Because one does not universally encompass both self and others, as well as the environment and its inhabitants (*niṣaya-vastu* and *pratisthāna-vastu*), one fails to understand that within a single speck of dust or a single thought, there is the mind-nature of all sentient beings and Buddhas. This is according to the Teaching.

It is said that this [work] clarifies the general principles of the sudden teachings throughout a single era, demonstrating to sentient beings that the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) is inherently present.

It establishes practice based on understanding by unifying the reliance [on the teaching] with the nature; thus, it brings the entirety of the nature to fruition as cultivation. Since one is not proficient in this, one cannot understand how the seeds are pervasive and how cultivation is pervasive.
Furthermore, when it is taught that the virtues of the Buddha-fruit are fundamentally complete within the causal mind, since one does not comprehend this, one cannot understand the fruit.

The universal manifestation of the Buddha’s interpenetration is entirely due to the fundamental principle; thus it is said that the Buddha taught that the environment and the beings within the realm of fruition are interpenetrating, and this is likewise due to the fundamental principle within the minds of sentient beings.
Since they do not realize this, they fail to understand that a single speck of dust or a single thought is itself the mind-nature of both the Buddha and sentient beings.
Although these four aspects exist, they are not expressed apart from the two meanings of teaching (*śāsana*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). As for the teaching, there are the following four:

The ten questions based on the "Contemplation of the Lower [Level]" serve as the foundation for the six questions on "Contemplating the Mind. Therefore, forty-six questions were further established to examine this point;
in each and every question, the principle that the three thousand realms are perfectly complete is revealed, thereby demonstrating the meaning that even insentient things possess Buddha-nature.
If one can understand even a single question among these without obstruction, [one has attained realization].

When these are dissolved away, one realizes that all phenomena are the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, not a single phenomenon is seen to be separated from it;
because the Dharma-realm is empty and pervasive, not a single phenomenon is seen to be obstructed by it. Is this not the Great Awakening?

Therefore, one penetrates and sees that within the Dharma-realm—the beings and Buddhas, the environments and their inhabitants—all things are of one substance and one mind, and there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm. Thus...

It was stated previously that "a single thought-moment is fully endowed [with all phenomena], not lacking even a single atom. This "single thought-moment being fully endowed" refers to the three thousand realms of the mind-only (*cittamātra*);
this "not lacking even a single atom" refers to the three thousand realms of form-only (*rūpamātra*).

Since form and mind are non-dual, and the essence of the environment and its inhabitants is one, although the term "three thousand" is not explicitly mentioned here, the intent of the three thousand realms is contained within it. These constitute the forty-six [sections].
Question: Since the Buddha-nature that does not arise through sequential generation is the thesis to be established, it is first interrogated;
since insentient matter is the attachment to be refuted, it follows next. Since the nature of both sentient and insentient things is thus solely mind, the nature of mind and phenomena is shown next;
because mental phenomena pertain to self-arising while the Buddha pertains to the other, the arising of the mind is questioned next.

Because the Buddha-dharma exists in the cause, it exists in the fruit; therefore, the next question concerns the Buddha. The Buddha is the primary retribution (*vipāka*), yet since the Buddha belongs to awakening, both the primary and the secondary are clarified.
Consequently, the next question concerns the distinctions of the lands where enlightenment is attained. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings do not transcend transformation and creation;
the phenomena of the ten realms are all that which is followed by conditions, while that which is able to follow is entirely True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, following this, the question on *tathatā* (suchness) is posed. Of the seven preceding meanings, all belong to the "Dharma-exposition" (*dharmadeśanā*).
While those of sharp faculties understand them, those of dull faculties have not yet clarified them; thus, they are further questioned by means of analogies.

The first forty questions concern the opening of understanding based on the teachings, serving as a response to the fault of not having understood the purport of the teachings. The subsequent six questions concern establishing practice based on that understanding.

Question: Regarding the fault of failing to observe the mind as previously stated, if we speak in terms of the general and the specific, the first forty-five questions are specific, while the final question is general.
As the subsequent text states: "Is it not the case that the final question clarifies the three non-differences?"
Question: Does the name "Buddha-nature" derive from the cause or from the fruit? If it derives from the cause, it is not the Buddha-fruit; thus, it cannot be called "nature. Question:

Is the name "Buddha-nature" permanent or impermanent? If it is impermanent, it is not "nature"; if it is permanent, it should not undergo transformation. Question: Is the name "Buddha-nature" common or distinct?
If it is distinct, it is not called "nature"; if it is common, it cannot be divided. Question: Does the name "Buddha-nature" pertain to the Mahāyāna or the Hīnayāna teachings?
Question: Is "small absence of nature" (the insentient) called "great absence of nature"? Question: Regarding the name "Buddha-nature," are there provisional and ultimate aspects?
Answer: To distinguish their characteristics by way of their substance:

first, regarding cause and effect, one should know that the Buddha exists only in the fruit [state], while the nature [of Buddhahood] largely resides in the cause; this is because the cause possesses the nature of the fruit.

That which is called Buddha-nature is the fruit; therein the environment and its inhabitants are interpenetrating and unified. This arises entirely from the fact that sentient beings possess it inherently within their causal stage;
thus, cause and fruit are non-dual. How could Buddha-nature be partial? Why then do you cling to such biased views regarding whether the insentient has nature or lacks nature?
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is the fruit and not the cause is called Nirvana; that which is the cause and not the fruit is called Buddha-nature. All things are thus.
1. "Sentient beings are Great Nirvana" refers to taking the cause from the perspective of the fruit; "Buddha-nature" refers to taking the fruit from the perspective of the cause.

2. Regarding the question of whether Buddha-nature is permanent or impermanent: if it were unchanging, it would follow the tenets of other schools which maintain that it resides in insentient things and is exclusively termed *dharmatā*;
would you then see Buddha-nature as impermanent? 3. Regarding the question of whether Buddha-nature is common or distinct: [it is] impartial.
All sentient beings equally share this [nature] which pervades all places, being neither internal nor external, and whether large or small, internal or external, its principle is one and the same.
How then can one distinguish between the insentient and the sentient, or between those with Buddha-nature and those without? Fourth question:

In the Small Teachings (Hīnayāna), there exists the doctrine of the insentient, yet the name "Buddha-nature" does not appear; in the Great Teachings (Mahāyāna), there is only... [the doctrine of universal Buddha-nature].

Regarding the discourse on Buddha-nature, there is no teaching that excludes insentient things. Now that Buddha-nature is explained as a central tenet of the Mahāyāna, how could the designation "insentient things lack Buddha-nature" still persist?
Fifth, concerning the provisional and the real: this question arises because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that tiles and stones do not possess [Buddha-]nature;
therefore, it uses the provisional and the real as a point of inquiry. Regarding the tiles and stones in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they do not...

Regarding the textual passages concerning nature (*prakṛti*): because they involve teachings that employ skillful means (*upāya*) while pointing toward the ultimate reality (*tattva*), there are passages difficult to reconcile regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the cause (*hetu*).

If the reality is such that the essence of the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*) is all-pervasive, then the conditions and the cause are not all-pervasive in terms of skillful means. If it were exclusively real, it would be like the three dots or the two birds;
if it were exclusively provisional, it would be like the seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River. Such is the relationship between the provisional and the real.
Each has its own destination. Question:

Are the names "insentient" (*niṣceṣṭa*) found in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings? Question: Within the great divisions of the Mahāyāna, are there provisional and ultimate [teachings]? Question:
Regarding the term "insentient," does it refer to form (*rūpa*), non-form (*arūpa*), or both? Question: Is the Buddha [identical to] insentient form and so forth?

Is it seen as arising from a view, or is it seen as being common to all views? One asks: since insentient things are subject to decay and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), is it also the case that the aggregates (*skandha*) are subject to decay and their nature is likewise so?
One asks: as for insentient things, which are the dharma-realm of form (*rūpa-dharmadhātu-āyatana*), is form also non-existent, or does it nevertheless exist?

Question: Regarding the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, previously the distinction was made based on *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature); now it is made based on the presence or absence of insentient things (*niṣceṣṭa*).
This is merely a matter of distinguishing between the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*bhūta-artha*) within the scriptural divisions to determine what constitutes Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

While the term "insentient thing" is restricted to the Hīnayāna school, it also appears throughout the Mahāyāna; for within the Mahāyāna, there exists the provisional teaching, and within that provisional teaching, there are insentient things.
The two questions—distinguishing between names and reality, and between the teachings and the distinction between sentient and insentient—are not about whether form is identical to mind;

rather, they are interrogations based on our school’s principle that form and mind are a single substance. If one clings to the view that the insentient lacks nature, then if it is said that the insentient is form, it would follow that there is no Buddha-nature in the insentient.
If it is said that the insentient is mind, then since mind is co-extensive with all things, and since form and mind are mutually identical (*sō-soku*), how could this be so?

"Is it not the Buddha-nature?"—this third question concerns whether insentient things, such as form and so forth, are identical to or distinct from form and non-form, and whether this constitutes the Buddha's vision.
Since the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom are the profound stillness of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there should be no duality. Is it for the sake of sentient beings' vision?
Since sentient beings are deluded and what they perceive is illusory, do these two [categories] follow delusion or follow awakening? If sentient beings and Buddhas were together...

4. Question: If the Buddha-nature does not exist because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) subject to arising and ceasing are subject to decay and destruction, then since the aggregates (*skandha*) and physical constituents of sentient beings are likewise subject to decay and destruction, would it not follow that the same applies to the body?

5. Question: Regarding the statement that insentient things are "form" (*rūpa*), this is said in reference to the relative relationship between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

Among the eighteen *dhātus*, although form, sound, and so forth belong to the five external sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), they partially enter into the *dharmadhātu* as mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*) within the sphere of the mind (*manobhūmi*).
Do these forms that are the objects of mental cognition exist or not?

If there is Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), and since internal form already exists, why does the form of grasses and trees not exist [within it]? If you say this form does not exist, then [consider] this...
If even a portion of the formless realm belongs to mind, and if that mind were non-existent, would you not then see that sentient beings are also non-existent?

Question: Have you ever heard the expression "mind-only" (*cittamātra*)? Answer: "Only" means that it is simply mind; it is not called "only" because there is something else different from it. Question:

Does the expression "mind-only" refer to the minds of both ordinary beings and sages? Answer: Whether referring to sages or ordinary beings, both positions entail faults. Question: What is the meaning of the term "mind-only"? Answer: It refers to the mind creating [all phenomena].
Is it that there is no mind, or is it that only the mind is created? Both positions entail faults. Question: Is it only mind, or is mind also only form?

If it is not only form, then form is not mind. Question: Is it that only names are created by the mind, or is there no mind? Or is it that only the mind is created? Both positions entail faults. Question:
Is it that only what is created by the mind exists, or is it the basis and the primary basis? Are the primary subject and object the same or different?
Yes. Regarding the initial question on "All is Mind Only," does one not recall that this passage appears in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*?

Since it is said to be "Mind Only," there is no phenomenon outside of mind; it is simply the One Mind. Whether referring to the sentient or the insentient, if one claims they are different, it contradicts the meaning of "Only."
The two questions do not hold, for "Mind-Only" refers precisely to the Dharma-realm where the environment and its inhabitants, the holy and the ordinary, are of one essence.
If one clings to the ordinary mind, the holy exists outside of the ordinary; if one clings to the holy mind, the ordinary is separated from the holy.
Therefore it is said that both the holy and the ordinary are at fault. This is solely because they cling to the notion that sentient beings possess only pure *tathatā* (suchness).
This [view] abandons the ordinary and retains only the holy; it is the fault of the "only-holy" mind.

If one follows the principle of our school regarding the "three thousand realms in a single thought," then this fault does not exist. Third question: Regarding the creation of existence, the mind is the creator and form is the created.
"Only" (*wei*) is a term signifying the absence of anything external. Since it is said to be "only mind," then both the creator and the created are entirely [mind].
Form is mind; outside of mind there is no form. Form and mind are not two. Now, regarding the phrase "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*):

if it means that only form is produced [and there is no mind that is form], then it would mean only form is produced [and producing form is form]. If one clings to either extreme, then form and mind become separated and distinct, and this is not "Mind-Only.
Question 4: Since it is called "Mind-Only," does it mean that it is only mind, or is it also only form?
Form is not mind; the Great Teaching holds that mind alone is real, for form and mind are non-dual.
Form is itself mind, and mind is itself form; as a single entity they are non-dual. How could there be form outside of mind? Fifth question:

All that is created by mind does not transcend the "dependent" (the environment) and the "supported" (the beings). This is precisely the support, and this is the supported. If you say they are identical, how could it be the Buddha-nature?

If it is claimed that "one" and "many" or "existence" and "non-existence" are different, then since that which is able to create is solely the mind, how could there be any difference in what is created?

Question: Does the nature of sentient beings vary according to their measure (quantity)? Answer: No. It is not that [the nature] is internal; if it were not so, it would not be called "nature. Question: Regarding sentient beings...
Regarding the four propositions concerning whether the deluded mind-nature is pervasive or non-pervasive and the divine self (*puruṣa*): are they identical or different? Question:

Do sentient beings possess nature (*prakṛti*) only as the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*, or also as the *dharmakāya* nature, and also as the *nirmāṇakāya* nature? Question: Is the fundamental delusion of sentient beings the delusion of the Buddha’s awakening?
Once the Buddha has awakened, does he awaken to the delusion of sentient beings? Question: How many Buddha-natures are there within the single body of a sentient being? Is it one Buddha-body?
Among these, what is the nature of birth?
The first question concerns the diversity of the dimensions of sentient beings—that is, the differences in the size, scale, length, and shortness of their physical forms.

If Buddha-nature were to vary according to these differences, it could not be called "nature. Conversely, if Buddha-nature does not vary according to these differences in dimension, then it would not be restricted to sentient beings alone.
Because it arises within the body, it is said that it is not so; yet, because it is not internal, it is not called "nature.
If one were to claim that Buddha-nature conforms to the measure of sentient beings, since Buddha-nature is one, how could there be such shifting changes and differing measures?

Second, regarding the question of whether the deluded minds of sentient beings are equal, this asks whether the nature of the deluded mind of ignorance is pervasive or non-pervasive. If the nature of delusion...

If the Buddha-nature is omnipresent, how could it not be omnipresent within insentient things? If you say it is not omnipresent, does this make it the same as or different from the four propositions of the non-Buddhists?
If you claim they are the same, the non-Buddhists themselves say, "The self is great and matter is small; the self pervades empty space.

Now, if you say it is not omnipresent, how can it be the same as theirs? If you say it is different, it is already inferior to the non-Buddhists, let alone being equal to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
Regarding the three questions on whether sentient beings possess Buddha-nature: there are three types of Buddha-nature; now I ask you:

what kind of nature do sentient beings ultimately possess? If you say it is the Dharma-body nature, since the Dharma-body is pervasive and the Dharma-body exists everywhere, why does it exclude insentient things?
If you say they possess the Retribution-body or Response-body natures, then the three bodies are mutually identical.
There is not a moment’s separation [between the bodies], as the *Miaole lun* (Treatise on Sublime Joy) states: “Because the Dharma-body pervades all places, the two bodies are ever-present.

Thus, it is said that they are “inherently complete” (*xingju*). Third, regarding the point that [the self-body] cannot be pervasive: one interpretation explains that this objection concerns the nature of sentient beings;

therefore, the self-body must naturally pervade the Dharma-body and the Reward-body. Fourth, the question: if sentient beings are fundamentally deluded, then what is the relationship between the delusion of sentient beings and the awakening of Buddhas? Regarding the assembly...

Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the dust; thus, what was originally pure has become turbid, and what was fundamentally awakening has become delusion.
The Buddhas, having reached the ultimate, turn their backs on the dust and conform to awakening; they return to the root and restore the source, so that delusion is forever lost.

Thus, while sentient beings are merely deluded and the Buddhas are awakened, though delusion and awakening differ, the substance of the principle remains one. Since the Buddhas [encompass] both the environment and its inhabitants...
Regarding the fifth question on the mutual identity of sentient beings and Buddhas: the wondrous nature of the three thousand worlds is perfectly interfused and universally penetrates all things;
thus, sentient beings and Buddhas mutually possess one another. To awaken to this is to become a Buddha; to be deluded about it is to remain a sentient being.

Since each and every sentient being and Buddha inherently possesses the nature of all sentient beings and Buddhas, how could one calculate that there are so many Buddhas within a single sentient being, or that there is only a single Buddha?
For how many lifetimes? Is the body in the Buddha-land the beginning or the foundation? Are the beginning and the foundation the same, or are they different?

Is the Buddha-land and the Buddha-body one or different? If they are one, there is neither subject nor object; if they are different, they are the same as ordinary beings. This asks about the birth within the divisions of the Buddha-land.
Furthermore, do the Buddhas each have their own respective abodes, or is there no land for a Buddha? Regarding what is encompassed by a Buddha-land, is it far or near?
Is that land identical to or different from the beings born therein, and are they common or distinct? Are the essence of the Buddhas and their Buddha-lands the same or different?
And as for the location of Sahā, is it common or distinct?
The initial inquiry concerning the "land" (kṣetra) refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* propagated by other schools, which manifests one aspect of the ten bodies of Vairocana.

Because they hold that the land is insentient and lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), it is difficult for them to explain how this land-body exists as something originally present during the causal stage, rather than arising only at the stage of fruition.
If it were to arise only at the stage of fruition, then it would be fundamentally... [incomplete].

There is nothing that exists now which is not an impermanent phenomenon. If it is said that the land-body is originally inherent within the bodies of sentient beings, then one would see the color of the land within sentient beings;
how then can it be said that the land lacks intrinsic nature? Since the beginning and the source are identical, cause and effect are non-dual.
Since cause and effect are non-dual, and since the fruit consists of the harmonious interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants, the cause likewise does not [lack this nature].
Regarding the distinction between the sentient and the insentient, if one says they are different, this is not what is elucidated by the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Second, concerning the Buddha’s reliance on the environment and the body: are the land upon which the Tathāgata relies and the body that relies upon it one or different?

If they were one, there would be no distinction between the reliant body and the supported environment; if they were different, they would be identical to the differentiated bodies and lands of ordinary beings. For your sake, [I shall explain].
Regarding the three questions—“Is one studying the Buddha studying the ordinary? and “Are the divisions of the Buddha-lands also places where beings dwell?”—there are three intended meanings.

As for the question, "Are the divisions of the Buddha-lands also places where beings dwell? this asks whether it is permitted for beings to be born and dwell together within these Buddha-lands, or whether they each have their own respective abodes.
This question asks whether beings and Buddhas each have their own lands in which they reside individually. [The text continues: "The Buddha has no... [omitted].

Regarding "land" (*bhūmi*): this question concerns whether the land where the *sattva-buddha* (the Buddha as a sentient being) dwells is distinct from the land where the *dharmakāya-buddha* dwells, or if there is no separate land for the Buddha’s body.

Although the question is threefold, it primarily clarifies that the *sattva-buddha* and the *dharmakāya-buddha* dwell together. Since the Buddha’s *rūpakāya* (the supported) and his *buddhakṣetra* (the support) are mutually identical (*lakṣaṇa-saṃvitti*), how could it not be so for the *sattva-buddha*?

By examining the Buddha through the *sattva*, the nature of insentient things is revealed. These four questions clarify that since the Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*), his lands must necessarily encompass all four [types of lands]. To speak of them as distant is to speak of the remote.

If we speak in terms of recent distinctions regarding the "near" and "far": the *upāya* (expedient means) realm is "far" because it lies outside the *sahā* (together-abiding) realm, and even the *śānta-prabhāsa* (tranquil light) realm is "far" because it lies outside the *bhūta-koṭi-vipāka* (true recompense) realm.
Conversely, if one realizes that phenomena are themselves the Truth (*tathatā*), then this very *Saha* world may be seen as either the *upāya* realm or the *bhūta-koṭi-vipāka* realm.
How could one seek the eternal tranquility apart from Gayā? Apart from the *śānta-prabhāsa* realm, there is no separate *Saha* world.
Therefore, one knows that the horizontal and vertical dimensions exist in only one place; thus, they are called "near.

Since the One already encompasses the Four, how can the land and the beings be either identical or different? Identity and difference pertain to the land, while commonality and distinction pertain to the people. Since the land is neither identical nor different [from the beings], who among the people could dwell together or dwell separately?
By means of the mutual fusion of the Buddhas, the non-duality of the beings is revealed. How could it be otherwise?

Whether taken collectively or individually, their principles are certainly not the same; whether as one or as different, how could Buddha-nature be divided? Regarding the five questions concerning the essence of the Buddhas and their lands:

previously, we discussed the similarities and differences by contrasting the living beings with the Buddhas; now, the Buddhas themselves pose these questions. That is to say, if we consider the essence inclusively, all are fourfold;
yet, while they share the same reality, they have never been identical. Furthermore, one should know that the horizontal and vertical dimensions reside only within this.
If they were identical in one respect yet different in another, then the Dharma-realm would be eternally identical and eternally different.
What, then, would be identical and what different? Ultimately speaking, when one seeks its body and land, they are utterly unfindable;

how, then, could there be the distinction between the sentient and the insentient? This has been a general discussion of identity and difference regarding the four lands. Second, the specific discussion:

Regarding the discussion of the similarities and differences between Śākyamuni’s co-residence and the various lands: is this the land of Śākyamuni distinct from them, or is it identical to the lands of all Buddhas?
Since the substance of these lands must necessarily be identical one to another, if they are identical, how can there be difference?
How then could one distinguish between the sentient and the insentient?
Question: When the Buddha attains enlightenment, does the land also attain enlightenment? Is it attained as being extensive or narrow? If it is not attained, there is a fault. Question:

Does the Buddha’s attainment of the realization of nature (jñāna-darśana) and the place where that realization arises constitute identity or difference? It cannot be asked [as either], for they are beyond these two. Question:

Are the Buddha’s attainment and the land’s attainment, along with their respective attainments and non-attainments, identical or different? Question: Are the Buddha’s three bodies (trikāya) and those various fruits identical or different?

Furthermore, regarding those various births, are they one or different? When asked about the Buddha’s accomplishment of the body and lands, what eyes, wisdoms, and visions are used to perceive the realms of self and others, and how are these established from beginning to end?

First, it was asked: when the Buddha accomplishes the lands, for a Buddha who has perfected the Path, the three delusions are utterly exhausted and the four virtues are perfectly luminous. The Dharma... [text continues].
The ultimate realization of the essence of the realms is the great function of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which follows and accords with the correct turning [of the wheel].
Thus, mountains, rivers, and lands do not fail to be perfected. This is what is meant by "the perfection of one is the perfection of all.

Since there is nothing within the Dharma-realm that is not this Buddha’s environment and its inhabitants (āśraya-sambhoga), can it be questioned whether these environments and inhabitants are broad or narrow? If one calculates that they are not perfected, the error would be immense.
Regarding the second question concerning the Buddha’s realization of the nature of reality: when the Buddha attained enlightenment, everything seen by his Buddha-eye was the body of Vairocana;

whereas what is seen by the flesh-eyes of sentient beings naturally manifests as various distinctions. Now, regarding what was seen by the Buddha upon attaining enlightenment, how could there be any difference between the animate and the inanimate?
Although the objects of the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind, are the same, the capacity to perceive them is inherently distinct.

The two meanings of "difference" and "non-difference" regarding delusion and enlightenment cannot be separated. Third, as for the question of whether the Buddhas are "formed" or "unformed"—this refers to the environment and its inhabitants (the *shèng* and *zhèng*).
The realization of the fruit by those various Buddhas of the ten directions is the unity of principle and phenomena;

their non-formation is precisely that sentient beings possess differences. Since the threefold non-differentiation explained in the Perfect Teaching (*yuánzōng*) is what is being elucidated, how could there be any difference?

Regarding the fourth question concerning the three bodies (trikāya) of the Buddha: whereas the previous third question addressed both the body and the land in general, this present question addresses the three bodies specifically.

The principle by which the Buddha’s attainment of the three bodies pervades his environment and inhabitants is identical to the principle by which those sentient beings in the ten directions attain the three bodies as their fruition;
however, there is a difference in that those beings must undergo the process of cultivation to realize them. Since the underlying principle is one and the same, how could it be...?
Distinguishing between the sentient and the insentient constitutes the five questions. Since the bodies and lands have already been established, what is ultimately accomplished?

The body is already Śākyamuni, and the land is already *Jikō* (Sambhogakāya). It is not that the four eyes and two wisdoms are absent; rather, the myriad phenomena are the Buddha-eye and the *Sarvajñajñāna*. True emptiness is profoundly tranquil;
how could there be further distinctions of self and other, or beginning and end, within the realm? Since there is no distinction of self and other, or beginning and end...
Second, do you distinguish between the sentient and the insentient?
Question: Are that which is produced by True Suchness (tathatā) mutually inclusive or not mutually inclusive? How is it in both cases? Question:

Does the essence of True Suchness pervade both the cultivated (xiu) and the innate (xing), as well as the body and the land, or are they unequal? Question: How does True Suchness transform in accordance with conditions?

Is it insentient? Is it eternally non-existent, or when will it come to exist? One asks: when True Suchness (tathatā) follows conditions, is it identical to or different from True Suchness itself once it has followed them?
Does it follow them eternally? One asks: is True Suchness originally existent or originally non-existent?
How is its coexistence with delusion characterized—identical or different?
First, regarding the question of whether the marks produced by True Suchness (tathatā) are mutually inclusive or not:

if True Suchness, following conditions, produces the myriad phenomena and they are mutually inclusive, then the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual; if they are not mutually inclusive, since that which follows [conditions] is one, how could that which is followed be two?
How can both cases be possible? Is it that the meanings of being inclusive and not being inclusive are established as two separate positions? Second, the question regarding True Suchness...
Regarding those who maintain that both the nature and the cultivation are practiced together, this question is precisely analogous to the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) interpretation:
the four virtues of cultivated merit (*shude*) serve as the dependent (*nōe*), while the four virtues of original nature (*shōde*) serve as the basis (*shoi*).

When both the dependent and the basis exist, and the body as the dependent equally corresponds to the land as the basis—these two meanings being identical—this constitutes the true characteristic of the body and land of Vairocana. This is the intended meaning of the present inquiry.
Since these are the characteristics of the body and land of Vairocana, how can you say that the insentient environment lacks intrinsic nature?

Third question: Sentient and insentient beings are both the entire substance of True Suchness, unchanging yet undergoing transformation. When it transforms into sentient beings, they possess intrinsic nature;
when it transforms into insentient things, they lack intrinsic nature, which would mean they are eternally non-existent. Yet, since they arise from this very nature through transformation...

If that were eternally non-existent, how could it ever become the Buddha-fruit of the future? Since the fruit is a fusion of the primary and secondary [receptacle worlds], the cause must likewise not be non-existent;
thus the four questions are established. Regarding the identity or difference of True Suchness (Tathatā) as it accords with conditions:

this asks whether the True Suchness that acts as the subject conforming to conditions is identical to or different from the True Suchness that serves as the object of such conformity; hence, it is said "according to."
Is the self identical to or different from True Suchness (*tathatā*), or does it follow [True Suchness] forever yet remain distinct from it?

If one says they are different, then this is not what is elucidated by the Perfect and Sudden Great Teaching; if one says they are identical, then one ought not to differentiate between the sentient and the insentient.
Since the five questions take the existence or non-existence of True Suchness as their inquiry, one should know that True Suchness and Buddha-nature are inherently possessed from the very beginning.
This is not merely the case now; therefore, it is said that they are fundamentally existent. If one were to say they are fundamentally non-existent, then the cause would not correspond to the fruit.

If we consider their coexistence, are they the same or different? Delusion and its nature share a common source, and the essence of delusion is identical to the true body—thus they are only the same, not different.

As for who is sentient and who is insentient, prior to the arousal of the mind, there is no truth that is not mundane and no mundanity that is not true; thus they are only different, not the same. Certainly, this is not what is being discussed here.

[The text continues as follows: ...the ear. [The interlocutor] asks: regarding the identity and difference between waves and water, their sequence and priority, their gain and loss, and the identity and difference between the real and the false—what are the analogies for these dharmas?

Regarding the identity and difference between the presence and disappearance of flowers seen by diseased eyes, and the space where those flowers appear—what are the analogies for these dharmas? Regarding the mirror-image and the luminous substance of its source...

How are the dharmas of beginning and end, sameness and difference, existence and non-existence, and their metaphors to be understood? Regarding the analogy of Indra’s Net, does it only illustrate the fruit, or does it also illustrate the cause?

Is there no cause for the fruit? Regarding the wish-fulfilling jewel body, does that body possess a land? Does it exist only at the stage of the fruit, or does it extend through the cause as well? How is this so?
The initial inquiry regarding the analogy of waves and water concerns moisture; how could it be divided between turbidity and clarity?

Water is the same, yet waves are distinct in their clarity or turbidity. As for the sequence of gain and loss: if one discusses the simultaneity of the wave and its moisture, there is no beginning of "before" or "after.
Speaking generally, when the entirety of the water becomes a wave, that is "before"; when the entirety of the wave returns to being water, that is "after."
Water originally has no waves; to have waves is "attainment" (得). Water has no name of "waves"; to lose [the water] is "loss" (失). Speaking in terms of the integration of phenomena:

arising from the True to produce the delusive is called "prior," and returning from the delusive to the True is called "subsequent. If one follows the realization of principle, it is called "attainment";

if one follows the confusion of phenomena, it is called "loss. The intent of the question lies in this: since the True is fundamentally without delusion, how could it be separated from the insentient? Second, emptiness is fundamentally without...
The flower exists because of an eye disease, yet it vanishes within emptiness; if the eye disease is removed, emptiness remains while the flower disappears into that emptiness.
Seeing the flower as distinct from its location is due to the eye disease; seeing emptiness as originally identical to that location is due to the removal of the eye disease.

Thus, whether emptiness appears as identical or distinct, or whether they both appear to exist or vanish—when these phenomena are spoken of in terms of their integration, they are merely the manifestations of a disease.

The empty sky is a metaphor for deluded sentiment; the flowers are a metaphor for the Buddha-nature. Upon the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which serves as the basis for both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu* and *adhiṣṭhāna-vastu*), the environment and inhabitants are fundamentally fused.
Due to the deluded sentiment of ignorance, this fusion becomes partitioned. Consequently, one perceives only differentiation and fails to see non-differentiation.

When the flowers remain, the sky is obscured by deluded sentiment; if that sentiment is removed, the partitions immediately dissolve into fusion. Therefore, where difference is perceived, there is in fact no difference.
Just as when flowers vanish in the sky, only the single Buddha-nature remains—how could it exclude the insentient?

Third, regarding the luminous essence of mirror-images: the essence of the mirror-image is the essence of the mirror’s clarity. As for the identity or difference between the original and the derivative:

the nature of the mirror’s clarity is the original ten realms, while the arising of images is the derivative ten realms. The essence of clarity is identical, yet the manifestations of the images differ in their beauty.

Regarding the mutual existence and non-existence of the "ugly" (the phenomenal) and the "prior" (the fundamental): the former is the beginning and the latter is the manifestation. When the manifestation exists, the fundamental is hidden; when the manifestation is extinguished, the fundamental exists.

Speaking in terms of the Dharma, if one discusses Buddha-nature, it does not exist [independently] within the dependent and the primary. How could the dependent and the primary exist apart from Buddha-nature? These four questions concern the pearls of Indra’s net (*indrajāla*).
The net of Indra is a metaphor for the mutual fusion of the dependent and the primary; by taking up one, all are fully encompassed, and each and every thing is so.
If non-obstruction refers solely to the analogy of the fruit, then the fruit would differ from its cause; yet if it also refers to the cause, the cause must necessarily encompass the fruit.
Therefore, since the primary and the secondary are mutually pervasive, how could the body and lands belong only to the fruit-stage? Fifth, regarding the "wish-fulfilling jewel body":

this jewel is shaped like a mustard seed or a grain of millet, composed of the seven treasures and *linglang* gems. It neither stores things within nor draws them in from without; it provides abundance or scarcity according to one's wishes.

Rain falls in profusion; this is now used as a metaphor. According to the needs of those to be saved, he manifests bodies within the ten realms, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel king rains down treasures according to one's wishes.
Because he preaches the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, it is called the "wish-fulfilling jewel body. Since a body must necessarily have a realm (kṣetra), it is said that "the body has a realm.
If one were to claim that the wish-fulfilling jewel body exists only in the state of fruition, that would be a mistaken view.
If this fruit is without cause, yet it is said to "pervade" the cause, please reveal its meaning. Thus it is asked: how does it pervade the cause?
If one knows that the fruit is such that body and land are non-dual, why then are there distinctions between the primary and the secondary in the cause?
Question: When a practitioner contemplates the mind, is the mind itself the object? How do the names of the "subject" (the grasper) and the "object" (the grasped) differ or agree?
Question: When a practitioner contemplates the mind, is it one or many? How do the mind and its objects differ or agree in being one or many? Question:

When a practitioner contemplates the mind, is he contemplating the mind alone, or does he also contemplate the body and the [buddha-]lands? Question: Does the practitioner’s contemplation of the mind occur within the context of afflictions, karma, and suffering?
Are the internal and external identical or different? When a practitioner contemplates the mind, is the Buddha-nature within the mind primordially pure or purified through cultivation?
When a practitioner contemplates the mind, are the mind, the Buddha, sentient beings, cause and effect, body and land, and all dharmic characteristics fused and subsumed such that all are identical?
This is truly because worldly people are not familiar with the great purport of the various teachings; previously, forty questions were posed to provide them with an opening understanding.
Furthermore, because worldly people do not skillfully grasp the entirety of cause and effect, self and others, and the dependent and the primary, they now look only to their own minds.
Therefore, six further questions are asked regarding the contemplation of the mind. This means that since one is already able to achieve a subtle understanding, one must establish subtle practice.

When the stages of understanding and practice support one another, the cooling pond can be reached. At the time of employing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), this mind is taken as the object of observation, while this very same mind simultaneously serves as the subject that observes.

Since both subject and object are the mind, and since consciousness and wisdom mutually illuminate one another—both being the three thousand realms—they each encompass all objects and modes of observation.
Though they are non-differentiated, they are differentiated for the sake of designation; thus, while there are two aspects, they are not two.
Second, because their essence is likewise identical, the *Yili* states: "Taking the mind as the object, the mind is also able to illumine it.

If subject and object are non-dual, and the object and contemplation are of one suchness, how can one distinguish between the sentient and the insentient? Second, regarding the question of whether the mind and objects are one or many:
when a practitioner contemplates the single mind within the myriad objects, is it not the case that the single mind pervades the myriad?

Because it is the object [of contemplation], one does not seek it through the categories of "one" or "many. This is because the practitioner, within the very moment of thought, contemplates the presence of the three thousand [realms];
thus, a single thought is itself the three thousand, and the three thousand are themselves a single thought. Because this wondrous reality is not fixed, it cannot be sought as "one";
therefore, it is not the same [as the conventional]. Because it cannot be sought as "many," it is not different [from the conventional]. (The third question.)

The practitioner contemplates the mind and realizes that the phenomena of the self and others, as well as the environment and its inhabitants (*shōjō-hō*), are all without exception the mind’s inherent endowment.

If one contemplates only the mind and does not contemplate the body and the land, this results in a state of differentiation and cannot be called the inconceivable realm (*fushigi-kyō*). As the *Kan Funi-mon* (Contemplation of the Non-dual Gate) states:

"Since the environment and its inhabitants both reside within the one mind, how could the one mind be divided into subject and object? Although there is no subject or object, they still rely upon [the mind]."
It is perfectly as it is; how could one distinguish between the sentient and the insentient? Fourth question:

regarding suffering, delusion, and karma—the three paths—the person of perfect enlightenment thoroughly understands that these three paths are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*). One must not seek the three virtues apart from the three paths.
If one were to seek pure *tathatā* apart from the three paths, how could this be called being "perfectly endowed with the single essence in non-duality"? Fifth question.
The Buddha-nature within the mind is both originally pure and newly purified.

Because the original purity of sentient beings' nature means that the environment and its inhabitants are identical as one, the fruit of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) is achieved, such that body and land are interpenetrated and function with sovereign mastery. Question Six:

This question concerns the mutual integration of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, as well as cause and effect, and body and land. If one realizes that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are identical—
Since the three thousand worlds and the three [realms] are without distinction, cause and effect, the body and the land—all phenomena—are mutually fused and encompassed;
from the beginning, there has never been a single dharma that is not identical.

If one can understand and contemplate in this way, then ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness, form and fragrance are extinguished into purity, and even the environment and inhabitants of the Avīci Hell are entirely present within the ultimate state of holiness.
One’s own mind and the body and land of Vairocana do not exceed a single thought-moment of an ordinary person at the lowest level.
If this is so, how could one calculate that insentient things lack Buddha-nature? Thus, it should be known that this single question summarizes all the preceding questions;
if one realizes the principle of non-differentiation, then within this one question all various obstructions can be resolved, and within a single answer, one has answered them all.

Question: Therefore, the subsequent text asks: "Is it not the case that by understanding the three non-differences in the final question, one immediately knows my own mind—that in every single moment, each and every sentient being is without exception identical to the body and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, and the self and other of the resultant virtues of Vairocana, such that they are mutually fused and mutually interpenetrating?"
Such answers to questions are inexhaustible; yet, to sever your doubts, I have provided this much for you.
You ask: "Why neither more nor less, but exactly forty-six? I reply: To strike down delusion, to strike down doubt, to strike down practice, and to strike down principle;

to penetrate the teachings, to penetrate the meanings, and to penetrate both oneself and others—one question is sufficient as an answer. Because of dull faculties, there are forty-six, and they correspond [to these needs].

The six stages of "immediacy" (*ji*) constitute the stage of partial realization (*pratyeka-sākṣātkriyā*), which is divided into forty-one positions; when combined with the preceding and succeeding stages, they total forty-six.
One should know that for each single question, it is capable of challenging the remaining forty-five, and each individual position must likewise possess all forty-six questions;
this applies even up to an infinite number of cases.

That which cannot be exhausted is used to briefly illustrate the extensive; that is to say, when one summarizes the profound purport of the teachings and contemplations of this entire school and sets them forth as the opening of a question, it is inexhaustible.
Because the guest intended to stop at this point, I have thus reached this much.

Regarding what the guest proposed, speaking in terms of the teaching: because he was not conversant with the purport of the teaching—that cause and effect are mutually integrated—he consequently failed to...

The Buddha-nature of insentient beings is ultimately non-dual; the three dharmas are without difference because True Suchness undergoes transformation and creation, just as water in its entirety becomes waves.

For this reason, there are the preceding forty questions. Speaking in terms of contemplation, because one does not skillfully encompass cause and effect, self and other, the environment and its inhabitants, but contemplates only one's own mind—viewing the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings solely as pure True Suchness—therefore [these questions arise].

The latter six questions are merely for the sake of hypothetical guests. If one were to pose further questions using the phrase "neither more nor less" as a pretext, the subsequent answers would be produced accordingly.
However, if one possesses sharp faculties, then even a single question regarding the principle of practice that dispels delusion and doubt is sufficient for all obstructions to vanish naturally;
what need is there for forty-six questions? What is called "striking" (*gong*) refers to breaking through and destroying [obstacles], while "penetrating" (*tong*) refers to thorough comprehension.

Furthermore, those who are deluded do so because they are confused by the phenomena that are the fruits of delusion, failing to understand the principle of the cause—that the mind is fundamentally complete from the outset and only becomes fully integrated upon reaching the fruit.
This delusion must be attacked. Since they doubt that insentient things lack intrinsic nature, this doubt must also be attacked.
Not only is their understanding thus, but even when establishing their practice and employing contemplation, they directly contemplate pure *tathatā* (suchness).

In this practice, one must critique the claim that True Suchness (tathatā) undergoes transformation to produce the environment and its inhabitants, thereby dividing them into two categories; this principle must be critiqued.
If one critiques these four points, it will encompass both the provisional and the real teachings, as well as the meanings concerning whether Buddha-nature is present or absent.

If one can skillfully understand the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" and establish one's practice based upon this, there will be no further need for the direct contemplation of a pure True Suchness.

Thus, one's own practice becomes unobstructed and flows through. Once one's own practice is established, there is no longer any following of the two divergent schools regarding *tathatā* (True Suchness) that would obstruct the Buddhist insight (*jñāna-darśana*) of later students;
therefore, it is said to "penetrate others. This first point refers to those of sharp faculties;
the next refers to those of duller faculties, as indicated by the forty-six [categories] and the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*). This is for the sake of addressing those of duller faculties.
It should be understood that those of sharp faculties are able to dispel obstructions and attain a vast, clear vision within a single question,

such that both their understanding and practice are simultaneously perfected; whereas those of dull faculties must rely on forty-six questions to fully comprehend the meaning of the perfect and sudden cause and effect,
as well as the principle of the mutual integration of the body and land and the objects of contemplation as elucidated in the sutras and treatises.

Regarding the identity of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*), the single principle from beginning to end, and the correspondence with the six stages of realization (*ṣat-samanvāgama*):
this refers not only to those of dull faculties but also encompasses the positions of the six stages of realization.

Because the principle is identical while phenomena differ, the six aspects of suchness (*ṣad-tathatā*)—as categorized in the *Fen-zheng-yao-chi*—are divided into forty-one stages, beginning from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogi-bodhi*).
The preceding principles—namely, the stages of name, contemplative practice (*ābhisamskāra*), semblance, and the subsequent ultimate—constitute forty-six [categories] in total when combined.
Although the number is the same when the questions are matched against their respective positions, this does not mean that one question is directly paired with one position.

This is because, regarding the questions, there is nothing they do not universally attack, and regarding the positions, there is nothing they do not fully encompass; this is also logically sound. Furthermore, it should also be...
To know that all questions range from the Buddha-nature to the contemplation of the mind is because their targeted meanings differ;
thus it is said that "one can refute the others," meaning that the refuter cuts through their doubts. If we discuss the questioning that performs the refutation, it is simply a single thought-moment.

According to the teaching of the three thousand [realms], one understands these three thousand through study and contemplates these three thousand through practice; how could they ever again refute one another?
From "Ya" up to "Immeasurable," it is likewise so; this refers to the meaning that these fetters cannot be exhausted from above.
