Compiled by the Venerable Jingxi Zhanran; edited by the Layman Liuju Yu Chunxi;
explained by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Shiju; reviewed by the Layman Sihu Shi Junming. A guest remarked:
"The principles established by you, O Benevolent One, are clearly different from what I heard in the past. When I first heard of them, I thought..."

Each blade of grass, each tree, each pebble, and each speck of dust possesses its own Buddha-nature and its own cause and effect, fully endowed with the provisional and ultimate conditions (*upāya* and *pariniṣpanna*).

If this were truly so, I would indeed find it unbearable. Why? Because while grasses and trees have birth and extinction, and pebbles and dust exist or do not exist according to the kalpas, they would not only be unable to cultivate causes to attain fruits;
rather, their Buddha-nature itself would undergo birth and extinction. This is something that all the world [would find inconceivable].
Since this is considered insentient, it is called "insentient"; it should not possess a nature. You have mistakenly used what is commonly transmitted in the world to challenge me;
you have utterly lost the ultimate principle. This is a most grievous error.

From the initial establishment of the thesis by Master Wen until the forty-sixth question, the principles established accord perfectly with the core tenets of the sutras and stand in stark contrast to what I previously heard—that insentient things lack Buddha-nature. My former understanding was that which I had not yet awakened to;
I had unconsciously slumbered, saying that insentient things have no nature. If this is so, then my present hearing differs from [my former view].

What I have heard in the past was so extraordinary that it left me utterly astonished. When I first heard it, I thought that every blade of grass, every tree, every pebble, and every speck of dust each possesses its own Buddha-nature;
that through the cultivation of oneself and others, from cause to fruit, each is fully endowed with the two causes of Buddha-nature—the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) and the *parikalpita* (provisional).
If this were indeed the case, then I, who am but a humble seeker of the Buddhist teachings, [would be deeply troubled].

Having briefly investigated the root source, I truly cannot bear to hear this doctrine. Why is this? For instance, consider grasses and trees: they sprout in spring, grow in summer, wither in autumn, and fall in winter;

their arising and ceasing never cease. As dust and pebbles follow along with their formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, and their existence and non-existence—if one were to claim that insentient things possess Buddha-nature, then not only would they be unable to cultivate causes to attain fruits, but they would also be seen as possessing Buddha-nature [in a manner indistinguishable from sentient beings].
"Is there arising and ceasing? The people of the world all say that these grasses, trees, and so forth are insentient;

therefore, they claim that what is insentient should not possess nature (*dharmatā*). Now, having heard the principle established by your reverence, which clarifies that insentient things possess Buddha-nature based on the fact that the substance of 'mind-only' inherently contains the three [natures] without distinction, I now repent, saying: I was mistaken to have followed what the world considers..."
"To transmit and practice this while it is difficult to realize benevolence is to lose the ultimate principle to an extreme degree; there is no error greater than this.
I said, "For what reason do you still maintain the name 'insentient'? The guest replied, "It is because I am reiterating my former view of delusion.

Now I also roughly understand that the principle established by you regarding benevolence is simply that the mind of every single sentient being is all-pervasive, and the nature is all-pervasive within the mind."
The nature and its manifestations are fully endowed, just like empty space; they are mutually unobstructed and each pervades both the body and the land.

Because cause and effect neither increase nor decrease, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. The term "world" here exhaustively encompasses the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages, as well as the environment and the inhabitants.
This passage records what was heard from the "Wild Guest" (Yekè), up to the point where it is argued that insentient things (*wuqing*) should not possess the nature [of Buddhahood].

Therefore, Jingxi severely rebukes him: "Since you have already accepted that all dharmas are the nature of the true cause (*zhengyin xing*) and have finished opening your mind to this understanding, why do you still maintain the designation 'insentient'?
Consequently, the Wild Guest below replies: "That was merely my own reiteration."
"The views I was deluded by in the past do not mean that I have now, having received instruction, understood the Buddha-nature;
yet the designation 'insentient' still persists. This reiteration of his initial delusion refers back to what he previously said:
"When I first heard the texts, I once held this delusion. This is Jingxi’s definitive assessment of the "Wild Guest" (Yekè).
The views of today must not be confused with those of the past; the situation now is not so. You already have a rough understanding of the principle established by the Benevolent One (the Buddha).

It does not depart from the intent of the "all-pervading" (ju-bian); that is, the preceding passage concerning the text on the "essence of the true cause of sentient beings being all-pervading" also uses empty space as a metaphor.
Thus, one realizes that there is no difference between the mind-only that understands the essence is inherent (ti-ju) and [the principle of] pervasiveness.
This is the meaning that the nature of the fruit-body and its lands (dharmakāya-bhūmi), which are non-distinct from the three [natures], permeates even such things as tiles and stones.
Now, first I shall indicate its general purport and subsequently provide a word-by-word commentary. Question:

Since this passage is precisely intended to lead one to understand that insentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why does it instead state that "it is simply that the mind of each and every sentient being is pervasive, the nature is pervasive," and so forth, up to "completely encompassing all"?
This is precisely the same as what Gushan (Zhili) stated regarding the manifestation of nature:
"Since this text states that the mind of every single sentient being is all-pervasive, why do you suddenly claim that the body and land themselves inherently possess the three thousand [dharmas]?

If the text were thus, it would indeed accord with Gushan’s view that the mind alone possesses the three thousand, whereas solitary form does not possess the three thousand. Answer: If one can penetrate and see the arising...

The Buddha, relying on the primary and secondary [receptacle and contained worlds], is complete within a single thought-moment; not even a single speck of dust is lacking, as he directly manifests his original nature as being of the same substance.

It is only because sentient beings are deluded by their perceptions and views, falsely engaging in discrimination, that they divide the material and mental realms, set the primary and secondary worlds in opposition, and differentiate between the animate and the inanimate. This is merely the conceptualization of sentient beings; truly, there is no difference in the Buddha-nature.

The Patriarch’s primary intent was to point out the nature of delusion to sentient beings; therefore, he frequently used the mind of sentient beings to demonstrate that Buddha-nature is all-pervasive.

Thus, he often stated that "form is precisely the mind. Furthermore, because he wished to establish the meaning of internal contemplation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā*) through what is immediate and essential, he spoke provisionally in terms of "mind-only.
Gushan failed to comprehend this meaning and merely saw one [instance] of the Patriarch’s...

The text is singular in its phrasing but concise in its meaning; it discusses pervasiveness in terms of the mind, leading some to claim that matter does not possess the three thousand [dharmas]. Therefore, the *Shiyi shu* (Treatise on the Ten Meanings) states:

"Superior persons firmly rely on the *Jinbi* (Golden Needle) when they say that the mind possesses the three thousand, and that those who discourse on Buddha-nature do so because that text precisely reveals the meaning of the pervasiveness of Buddha-nature.
Since 'Buddha' is spoken of in relation to sentient beings, it frequently clarifies that matter is identical to the mind."
Therefore, one should know that if one believes that all forms are mind, it establishes the principle that even insentient things possess Buddha-nature;

it also serves to establish the principle of internal contemplation. Thus, for the time being, we discuss this in terms of "mind-only," because the scriptural texts of the various teachings are primarily directed toward sentient beings of the lower realms and therefore mostly clarify "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
This does not mean that those [insentient things] are unilaterally subsumed within the one [mind].

Regarding the passage stating that "the environment and its inhabitants, from the Buddhas down to a single mote of dust, are not deficient," how can one explain the phrase "forming the three thousand without deficiency"?
As for the explanation that "it invariably subsumes the external back into the internal," the text simply states that the mind of every single sentient being is both pervasive and universal.

Here, "mind" refers to the aspect of following conditions (*suiyuan*), while "nature" refers to the aspect of non-changing (*bubian*). Now, this points specifically to the aspect of following conditions.

When the mind remains unchanging in its proper place, it is called "nature" (xing); thus, we speak of the "mind-nature. That both mind and nature are all-pervasive demonstrates the meaning of the essence’s magnitude (ti-liang).

That the mind is endowed [with all] and nature is endowed [with all] demonstrates the meaning of the essence’s virtues (ti-de), which is precisely the principle of the aforementioned "the body is endowed with the sole mind" (shen-jue-wei-xin).
Since this pervasiveness is identical to the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), it is like empty space—unobstructed and each pervading its respective counterpart.

There is no difference between the sentient being and the Buddha; only in this way can one know that the sentient being and the Buddha are identical within the single, perfect fusion of the three thousand realms.
This is because the substance of their nature is like space, mutually fusing without obstruction.

Therefore, those instances of mutual, perfect fusion and pervasive entry—whether referring to body and land, or cause and effect—are as follows: the mind arises in the state of cause, while the Buddha exists in the state of fruition.
Because the three dharmas of cause, fruit, and practice are equal, there is neither increase nor decrease;
thus, by analogy with my own mind, the causes and fruits, bodies and lands of all sentient beings and Buddhas are each universally interfused and entirely equal.
Therefore, how could Buddha-nature not pervade even insentient things? Thus, the permanence of worldly phenomena is cited as proof.
I said, "Observing what you have seen, it seems you understand the general principle; why not attempt to answer that previous question?

The guest said, "Master, you yourself previously stated that if one contemplates a single question, all obstructions will naturally dissolve. If I were to provide an answer, I would do so by answering one response to encompass all questions;
in that case, how could there even be a 'single question'? I said, "Please explain your meaning. The guest replied, "I shall return [to that point]."

If one grasps the intent behind these various questions and thereby dissolves all obstructions, this itself is called an answer; why resort to the laborious method of responding to each question individually?
For what reason? Is it not because I previously did not accept the doctrine that insentient things possess Buddha-nature, whereas I now do accept it?
This is precisely the answer.
This is truly because this rustic guest has a rough understanding of the principles established by you; he has grasped that the nature of mind is universally present, like empty space.
He cites the *Lotus Sūtra*’s teaching on the permanence of worldly phenomena and how the provisional and the real are fully encompassed within the Buddha-nature.

His insight seems to reflect a partial knowledge of the major tenets of the scriptures regarding the provisional and the real, and the presence or absence of Buddha-nature. Thus he says of his previous question: [it was based on this].
Since you are already able to grasp the general purport [of our discussion], why not attempt to answer one of the forty-six questions posed previously?
As stated above: "If one can understand even a single question of mine, all obstructions will naturally dissolve;
the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, and one will attain a vast, clear vision. You, sir, have already stated that you understand one question.
Thus, all obstructions will naturally dissolve. Now, by providing a single answer that resolves all questions, how could there even be a "single question" remaining?
Jingxi, because [the Master] stated that this one answer universally answers all questions, requested an exposition of its meaning. The guest said:

"I have thoroughly examined the various questions posed previously; in each and every one, [the Master] has manifested that the three causes are all-pervasive and that the three dharmas are without distinction."
The teachings of the various schools—whether provisional or real, fragmented or partial—struggle to reveal the perfect and real principle.

When such manifold obstructions are thus dissolved and one reaches the point that even insentient things possess Buddha-nature, this itself constitutes the answer. Why then should one laboriously elaborate upon each individual question?
Therefore, the direct response to the inquiry is as follows: "What is it? For how could these many questions not arise from my own inability to receive [the teaching]?

Regarding the doctrine that "sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature," your recent letter has accepted this meaning; this single response thus serves as a comprehensive answer to all the questions. I said:
"In broad outline it is so, yet I do not yet understand your underlying intention. The guest replied: "The principle you have established pertains to the various Great Teachings."

It is difficult to describe in full detail; I shall provide a brief discussion here, hoping for your gracious attention. Is it not the case that by understanding the three non-differentiations of the final question, one immediately knows my heart?

That in every single moment, each and every sentient being is without exception identical to the body and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, and the self and others of the resultant virtues of Vairocana—mutually fused and mutually entering—and that both I and all sentient beings possess [these qualities].

Because this nature is called "Buddha-nature," its essence pervades all creation, pervades all transformation, and pervades all that is gathered. Yet worldly people do not understand the substance of the Great Teaching;
they speak only of "insentient things" and do not say they possess this nature. Therefore, one must state that insentient things possess this nature.

Once one understands that this nature is all-pervasive, one realizes that the Buddha-fruit possesses the causal natures of both self and others, and that my own mind possesses the resultant virtues of all Buddhas.
When viewed from the perspective of the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom at the stage of fruition (*phala*), there is only the Buddha and no birth.

Within the causal stage (*hetu*), if true wisdom and the true eye are in profound accord, then birth itself is entirely the Buddha; there is no separate Buddha apart from fruition. Therefore, outside of birth there is no Buddha.

Sentient beings grasp at this through the ego-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), whereby there is no Buddha and only birth. Only the initial resolve (*prathama-citta*) that can believe the teaching and look up to the principle is also non-arising. Only...
When the Buddha is absent, there is neither birth nor the illumination of the Buddha; yet when the Buddha shines upon it, cause and effect become manifest.
One should know that sentient beings possess only the principle within their delusion, while the Buddhas possess both the phenomena and the principle within their awakening.
Sentient beings take phenomena as their object, whereas the Buddhas realize the principle. Although delusion and awakening differ, the essence of phenomena and principle remains the same.
Because they are one, when a single Buddha attains enlightenment, there is nothing within the Dharma-realm that is not the environment or the body of this Buddha.
Since it is so for one Buddha, it is likewise for all Buddhas. Yet sentient beings, within the very environments and bodies of the Buddhas, give rise to divergent views;

they perceive suffering and joy, ascent and descent, and each individually calculates these as their own bodies and lands—pure or impure, manifesting clearly as formation and destruction. Is this not precisely what you intended to ask?
"Not so; I say, 'Excellent, excellent! You have swiftly grasped this meaning. Indeed, you can comprehensively understand the structural framework of all questions.
This already answers hundreds of thousands of millions of questions—how could it be limited to only forty-six?"
The narrator’s words of understanding, acceptance, and faith were brief though they may have been; yet, in the end, he did not fully comprehend the underlying sentiments of my former attachments.
He must surely now feel a sense of great relief, seeing clearly and penetratingly into the *dharmadhātu*. As a guest, I shall no longer restrain myself and thus advance these words:
"The principles you have established pertain to the various Great Teachings; these very principles are identical to those addressed in the preceding questions."
I have briefly discussed the meaning of this; it is understood that the final question concerns the non-differentiation of the three [natures], and the answer follows from this.

Because one understands the meaning of the non-differentiation of the three and so forth, one attains liberation through inquiry. Therefore, one fully grasps the meaning of the preceding teaching regarding contemplation;
one then personally realizes that the nature of my mind’s coming and ceasing is universally inclusive. This is the realization of the aforementioned integration of cause and effect.
"Observing oneself and others within one's own mind" refers to the principle that the Buddha, sentient beings, and the self are of one essence.
"Simply stating that insentient things possess Buddha-nature" refers to grasping the essential meaning of the Great Teaching.

"Once the pervasiveness of nature is realized, cause and effect become manifest" refers to grasping the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching on the virtues of the fruition. From [the stage of] "correspondence"...
To know that sentient beings are merely principle and that all Buddhas are likewise present is to comprehend the meaning of the mutual fusion of the Buddha’s manifestations;

while they differ from sentient beings, this general outline is thus. We shall now explain them in sequence. First, regarding the meaning of the Dainichi Nyorai’s (Vairocana) resultant virtues—the body and mind, the environment and its inhabitants (*shin-jō*)—these are the three thousand realms realized as the fruit, all of which are termed "Eternal and Blissful. Therefore, as for form...
Whether it be the mind (*citta*), its basis (*āśraya*), or the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*), all manifest the four virtues;
because the three are without distinction and the arising of the mind is fundamentally identical, self and other attain mutual fusion and mutual entry in equality.

Since this discussion of self and other is based on their mutual fusion, it should be understood through the mutual relation of the three dharmas as self and other: either the mind is taken as "self" and the Buddha as "other," or the Buddha is taken as "self."
That the mind arises as mutually integrated with others refers to the aforementioned "each and every one being all-pervasive";

this is precisely what is meant by the "essential point" known as "perfect integration and universal entry. "Equality" means that there is no increase or decrease in the body, the land, cause, or fruit.
Because they are equal, there is no increase or decrease; all sentient beings possess the nature of the fruition-stage person.
Therefore it is said: "I and all sentient beings all possess this nature; for this reason it is called Buddha-nature. This nature universally creates;
"creation" means to fully possess—that is, to fully possess all matter and mind, both the environment and its inhabitants. It universally transforms;

"transformation" means to undergo change—that is, to transform and create all matter and mind, both the environment and its inhabitants. It universally encompasses; since it is fully possessed as that which is transformed, it is fully...
"Transformation" means that by raising up a single part, the whole is fully encompassed; there has never been a single dharma that is not subsumed within it.

This is the principle of observing one's own mind as the Buddha and as sentient beings, universally grasping the environment and its inhabitants, both self and other. Next, regarding the summary of the great purport of the various teachings mentioned above:
that which is elucidated and demonstrated by the great purport of all teachings is that the essence of Mind is inherently endowed with all things from the beginning.
It is simply the Buddha-nature; however, because worldly people are deluded, they do not follow it from the perspective of the fruit.

They speak of sentient beings as having [the nature] and thus lose sight of its essence, which is pervasive throughout both the sentient and the insentient. They speak only of the "insentient" and do not say that there is "nature.
Therefore, what you have now established must indicate the pervasiveness of the essence within that nature, stating that "the insentient have nature"—this is the great purport of these teachings.

The Buddha taught the three meanings to clarify that the fruit-virtue is inherent within the causal nature of the mind; he merely intends for sentient beings to fully give rise to cultivation from within their own nature.

Once one understands that the essence of nature is fundamentally pervasive throughout the three [times] and without distinction, one realizes that the Buddha-fruit possesses the causal nature of both self and others—that is, the fruit is already present within the cause. Thus, my own mind possesses the fruit of all Buddhas.

Virtue is precisely the cause inherent within the fruit; thus, the cause and the fruit are one and the same three-thousandfold world. When the principle of the three-thousandfold world is fulfilled, it is realized as the fruit.
When observed with the eye of wisdom that is ultimately perfect and luminous, then empty truth is darkly quiescent, and there is no longer any distinction between self and other or mutual seeing;
only the single wisdom of True Suchness remains. Therefore, [this state] belongs to the Buddha alone.
The term "arising" (*sheng*) may also apply to the stage of partial realization (*fenzhengwei*).

If, within the causal stage, true wisdom and the true eye are in profound accord, this phrase encompasses both the stages of contemplative practice (*guangxing*) and semblance (*xiangsi*). In these stages, wisdom and the eye are both in accordance with reality, illuminating and seeing according to reality;
it is like one who has just entered the [Ten] Stages and is thus able to see the fused and subtle three thousand realms, though this is still viewed in comparison to the subsequent stages.

The difference lies only in clarity and obscurity; yet it is said that they correspond in darkness because, within the hindrances, ignorance has not yet been shattered and one cannot yet manifest vision.

Nevertheless, by being darkly united with it, one is also entirely born as a Buddha. Since all dharmas perceived by the Buddha are the three thousand realms, how could there be any fruit outside of sentient beings?
The two lines following "sentient beings" clarify the principle of *ri-ji* (the identity of principle). Sentient beings... [text ends]... are the principle itself.

The causal mind for birth is such that there is no principle it does not embody; yet, throughout long kalpas, it employs these principles without knowing them, merely following the deluded self to grasp at and become attached within the triple world.
Thus, while there is no Buddha, the initial mind arises at the lowest level of names.
Because this initial mind of names receives the teachings, it gives rise to perfect, eternal, and correct faith in the principle; though the principle has not yet been seen, [it is so].
I look up to you with admiration as you have fully opened the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), whereby principle (*li*) harmonizes with phenomena (*shi*).

You are able to realize that all dharmas are none other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and that there is neither arising nor non-arising; yet, these are merely names. Those who have not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*) remain within the realm of names;

those who have entered the stages possess the power of "extinguishing-illumination" (*wangzhao*). Now, this extinguishing-illumination resides within the realm of names—precisely because it is illumination, it is extinguished.

When both dependent origination and its cessation are utterly extinguished, the provisional names of "sentient beings" and "Buddhas" vanish; yet, as one illuminates all phenomena, cause and effect remain perfectly distinct.
Regarding the four meanings—wherein sentient beings perceive only the principle (*li*) while the Buddhas attain the phenomena (*shi*), and so forth—as stated in the *Miaoxuan*:
"Sentient beings attain the phenomena, while the sages attain the principle. Furthermore, regarding the sages...
Regarding the attainment of phenomena, there is a rational explanation in the *Jishi Chao* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) which states:
"The attainment of sentient beings is the phenomenon of principle; the attainment of sages is the principle of phenomena. What the sages know, sentient beings do not know.

Sages attain the phenomena of cause and effect, such as transformation and response for the sake of others; sentient beings, however, only attain the principle within delusion that is neither cause nor effect."
Sentient beings have not only failed to awaken, but they do not even recognize their delusion; therefore, it is said that there are only the phenomena and principles within delusion.
The Buddhas have not only already awakened, but they also manifest delusion; thus, it is said that they possess both the phenomena and principles within awakening.
Although delusion and awakening differ, they do not transcend the ten realms and thousand suchnesses; in a single mind or a single speck of dust, there is no place that does not fully embody them.

The three thousand [realms] are thus because fact and principle, beginning and end, and essence and manifestation are one; therefore, when a single Buddha attains enlightenment, he realizes the essence of the Dharma-realm and acquires its function.
Relying upon and following the transformation of the primary and secondary [receptacle and sentient worlds], the realization of one constitutes the realization of all.

There is nothing within the Dharma-realm that is not the primary or secondary support of this Buddha. Since it is so for one Buddha, the same applies to the attainment of the fruits by each and every Buddha; hence, they are called "all Buddhas."
All that sentient beings perceive is due to their having, from the very beginning, turned their backs on the nature of the Three Virtues;

being solely deluded and flowing against the current, they revolve through the three realms of existence. Within the state of equal Dharma, they give rise to the false imaginings of self and other, perceiving distinctions in form and characteristics.
Consequently, in all places of suffering and joy, rising and sinking, each and every one reckons those as their own body and land.

The Buddha is eternally fused [with all beings], yet sentient beings create their own barriers; thus, purity and defilement appear distinct, and the processes of formation and destruction reside therein.
Regarding the two phrases you asked about at the end, they constitute my concluding response. As for "I say" at the beginning, it serves as a seal of approval and a summary.
The guest said, "I nearly failed to meet a benevolent person; otherwise, this life would have been spent in vain. Must one rely on this view to attain supreme fruition?

I replied, "If you wish to cultivate the teachings, yet the study has not yet been completed—if you do not first become proficient in the doctrinal path of our own school, you will be unable to thoroughly investigate the beginning and end of the practice gate.

How then could you possibly encompass the entirety of the principles of teaching and practice, or the phenomena of delusion and wisdom, cause and effect, the environment and its inhabitants, and the mind and its dharmas?"

I employ this as the primary contemplation for the initial mind of ordinary beings; yet what you have grasped seems to be empty, for your estimation of the Way of contemplation remains as formless as a phantom.
The guest asked: "What is this 'Way of contemplation'? Who is your benevolent teacher? Upon what Dharma do you rely? I replied:
"Have you not heard of the Great Master of Tiantai, who personally received the transmission at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and attained wondrous awakening at the Great Awakening (Dafu)? He is my teacher."
The *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) is the Dharma it inherits; it takes twenty-five factors as its preliminary expedients (*pūrvayoga*) and ten factors as the vehicle (*yāna*).

One contemplates ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*), and whether these contemplations progress or regress depends on how these ten objects mutually trigger one another—this is the general outline of this path of contemplation.
For now, let us merely identify the first of the ten vehicles, the wondrous object (*viṣaya*), as the various other vehicles and objects need not be discussed here.
The guest said, "Excellent! I shall admire this as my reliance for eternal kalpas. 'Ji' (near) means proximity;
if one does not encounter a benevolent person while near him, this life will be spent in vain and lost.
Might it not be that even such a loss would be of no benefit? Now, having heard the discourse on full ordination and the principle of non-differentiation, though I am spared [from immediate harm]..."
"Will this fault necessarily be remedied by practicing and realizing according to this principle so that one may surely attain the supreme and wondrous fruit?

I replied: "Regarding those for whom the ultimate teaching has not yet been fully disseminated, this merely indicates the first of the ten vehicles, which is the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
The details are as found in the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation); therefore, the subsequent text says: 'For now, let them recognize the first of the ten vehicles.'"
It is merely a wondrous realm; there is no leisure to discuss the various realms of other vehicles, which is why it is said that the teaching is not yet complete.
If one wishes to investigate in detail the beginning and end of the practice gate (*caryāmārga*), one must be well-versed in the doctrinal path of this single school.

Furthermore, the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) transmitted here takes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as its backbone, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as its guide, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* as its supporting branches.
Taking the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as the warp for contemplating the Dharma, it cites various sutras to increase faith and various treatises to assist in the accomplishment of contemplative mind;
with the sutras as the warp and the dharmas as the woof, they are woven into a single volume unlike any other.
Therefore, five chapters are indispensable for generating sublime understanding, and for subsequent practice, twenty-five methods must all be employed as the guiding framework.

Thus, one takes the ten vehicles and ten objects as the primary cultivation. If one does not understand the beginning and end of this gateway of practice, how can one know its commencement and conclusion?

As for what constitutes the beginning and end: the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states that from beginning to end, it is simply contemplating the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and entering into the three virtues, even pointing back to oneself.
This does not exceed the five summaries, up to the twenty-five dharmas.
The ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) and ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) of the skillful means (*upāya*), from cause to fruit, culminate in the ultimate convergence of self and others within the secret treasury;

this constitutes the beginning and end of a single period [of the teaching]. Regarding the "teaching, practice, and the mind of the Dharma," there are six pairs, which represent the intent of the inclusion of all phenomena within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
As it is said: "Inclusion comprises all principles, delusions, wisdom, stages of practice, and teachings—these are the six. Thus, "teaching and practice" refer to these six.
Regarding the two matters within this—principle and phenomena—the two types of three thousand (the three thousand of principle and the three thousand of phenomena) encompass all principles;
the remaining five are phenomena. "Delusion" refers to the three delusions; "wisdom" refers to the three contemplations. "Stages" encompass both cause and fruit; "cause and fruit" constitute a pair.
"Support and expression" means that cause and fruit pervade the ten realms of support and expression. "Mind and dharmas" refers to the creating mind and the created [dharmas].

If the Dharma were not received through the ten chapters of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), from its beginning to its end, how could one fully comprehend and encompass such teachings as those mentioned above?

To enter the contemplation of the dharma within a single thought-moment (*ekacittakṣaṇa*) and to realize the three thousand realms therein constitutes the primary beginning for cultivating contemplation at the stage of the initial mind.
You, my disciple, have grasped the principle that the aforementioned three [realms] are without distinction.
It seems as though his mind is empty and vast; he merely understands intellectually.

This time, your observation of the Way within your own house is still like that of *wangxiang*—*wangxiang* being a description of something not yet real. The guest said: "The subsequent follows from the preceding.

Since I reckon that your observation of the Way is not yet clear, I have posed three questions: the first concerns the observation of the Way, the second concerns the lineage of the teacher, and the third concerns the [place of] origin."
In response to your inquiry, I first address the lineage of transmission: in the past, at the wondrous assembly on Vulture Peak, he personally received the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
in this life, he inherited the teachings from Nanyue and attained wondrous realization under Dazhu Huike.

As for the "separate transmission," when Jingxi responds regarding his own lineage, tracing it back from Zuoxi to Zhiyi, he is the fifth-generation descendant; yet today [you] refer to the Great Master of Tiantai as a "high" [ancestor].
The Patriarch is his teacher, while Zuoxi (Zhanran) is his father-teacher. He answers the Dharma he inherited through the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).
"Mahā" (Great) serves to distinguish it from the gradual, the indeterminate, and the minor *zhiguan*, as well as the twenty-five methods.

In the passage below, he answers regarding the path of contemplation; the twenty-five methods are the preliminary expedients (*pūrvayoga*) corresponding to the ten vehicles, which are the proximate expedients.

Regarding the ten dharmas that constitute the vehicle: from the inconceivable realm up to the tenth, the departure from attachment to dharmas—these ten dharmas combined form the Mahāyāna, which is called "the contemplator" (*nirūpaka*).
It takes the ten realms as its "objects of contemplation" (*nirūpya*). Furthermore, each individual realm possesses these ten vehicles;
the mutual arousal of the ten realms is exemplified by the arousal of afflictions while contemplating the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*).
All such matters as the sequence and non-sequence of the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* should be properly distinguished when the object arises within the meditative state;
one must know what to advance and what to avoid so as not to cause confusion. This is merely a general outline. Furthermore, this concerns only the first of the ten vehicles:
the inconceivable object (*acintya-viṣaya*). Therefore it is said: "The various questions," for that which is elucidated by these questions does not go beyond [this].
The Buddha-nature of the insentient is the great purport of the Three Thousand Worlds; yet, regarding the contemplative methods of the Initial Vehicle, it has not yet been fully elucidated.
As for the various realms of the other vehicles, I have not had the leisure to discuss them in detail.
This rustic guest, having received the purport of the supreme path of contemplation, feels a profound sense of admiration and reverence, taking it as his reliance for eternal kalpas.
The guest said, "I have frequently heard the lectures of various masters who expound the Mahāyāna, yet they still regard the Buddha-nature of insentient things as a separate view. Why is this so?
I replied, "There is a reason for this. These individuals have previously encountered the term 'insentient' from the Hīnayāna and have also seen the expression 'Buddha-nature' in the Mahāyāna.
Having lost the discourse on universal integration that they were propagating, they have abandoned Nirvāṇa and empty space."
This analogy fails to reach the principle that the three causes of cultivation and nature are neither separate nor unified, and that there is no difference between the unawakened and the Buddha.
Erroneously imitating the transmission of insentient words, one instead challenges the school’s own doctrine of Mind-Only.

By citing exclusively the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s discourse on tiles and stones, one fails to fathom the intent behind the appearance and disappearance of various time-periods and divisions—like a child of noble lineage who lacks a lifespan and has strayed into a state of lost childhood.

To return home in vain while still deluded about one’s own clan is like receiving a noble rank yet remaining ignorant of one’s ancestors; such a person is no different from a dead man wearing jeweled necklaces.
To employ such merit as a purpose, or to treat these necklaces as the mark of the Dharma, is a total confusion regarding the fundamental.

If you should encounter such individuals, you ought to question them with the aforementioned intentions: "Are the scriptures you propagate those of the Mahāyāna or the Hīnayāna? Even this much they will fail to grasp.
The Hīnayāna has already been discussed as previously stated.
My guest, having received this exposition on the stages of practice (*caryā*) within one school, was inwardly delighted and sincerely convinced.

He then raised a question regarding the divergent views held by various Mahāyāna masters concerning their respective traditions, specifically the distinction they draw between insentient matter (*niṣcit-sattva*) and Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
What is called "seeing" is merely the false conceptualization of this insentient Buddha-nature as being insentient and lacking Buddha-nature;
because the Buddha-nature does not pervade the insentient, the nature of the sentient and the insentient are deemed different, and thus it is called "distinctive seeing.
Master Ji takes the very object of their delusion to refute them, for these individuals have previously studied the four Āgamas of the Hīnayāna.
To exclusively and narrowly manifest the name "insentient" (*niṣceṣṭa*) while not asserting that this insentience possesses Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*),
and to observe that within the various Great Teachings there are expressions of "Buddha-nature" which speak only of Buddha-nature without establishing the existence of insentient things— yet,

while insisting that the categories of "insentient" and "Buddha-nature" are vastly different, one consequently forgets the core principle propagated by the *Avataṃsaka*: the mutual interpenetration and integration of the primary and secondary realms (*śāsanadeśana* and *pratītyasamutpāda*).

Such talk is delusory, for while it treats the fruit as a substantial entity, it fails to believe that cause and effect are fundamentally unified; thus, it leads to the abandonment of the metaphors of *nirvāṇa* and space.

It fails to realize that the principle of the nature of beings (*zhòngshēng lǐxìng*), the true cause of Buddhahood (*zhènyīn fóxìng*), pervades all places—being neither internal nor external—and furthermore, it does not comprehend the meaning of the union and separation of the three causes:
the causal, the conditional, and the consummating. While the true cause pervades all places, the conditional and consummating causes must necessarily accompany it.

Taken together, these are simply termed the "direct cause" (*hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding the principle that the Buddha’s birth is inconceivable and without distinction [from sentient beings]:

since the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the fruition stage pervade the arising of the mind, how could this not be so? Therefore, to perversely imitate the transmitted teachings of the Hīnayāna—which speak of the arising and ceasing of insentient grasses and trees, or the existence and non-existence of tiles and stones—and to use them to challenge the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which is the very doctrine one's own school propagates, is a grave error.

Those who exclusively cite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s discourse on tiles and stones as the definitive proof for the teaching that "all phenomena are mind-only" do so because they fail to understand the provisional nature of the timing and sections [of the teachings], the meaning of whether the Buddha-nature is manifest or not,

and the intended meanings of "appearing and disappearing," "either provisional or real," and "clarifying both together. It is precisely because tiles and stones are insentient that [the sūtra] clarifies both [sentience and insentience].
The question of whether the Buddha-nature within the intermediate state possesses provisional or ultimate meaning—how could it be considered final?

As for the ten phrases above, their textual meanings arise from one another. Below, four points are raised to refute the forgetting of the source; although these explain the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), what benefit do they bring to people?
This is like the analogy of a son of merit who lacks a lifespan, as cited from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Second.
1. "Those who have lost their way in youth return empty-handed": "weak" refers to the young; "lost" means to have strayed.
To lose one's home in youth and subsequently return is like being lost to one's own kin, as Zhuangzi said: "Those who have lost their way in youth do not know how to return.

Three such cases are recorded in the *Liang Shu*, in the biography of Hou Jing, where individuals attained noble positions yet remained ignorant of the affairs of their ancestors. Four such cases are those who died.
The analogy of people wearing necklaces is from the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*. To illustrate the vastness of the Dharma they propagate:

though their merit leads them back to receive noble status and they wear necklaces, because they do not know that the fundamental principle of Buddha-nature is originally all-pervasive—like a lifeless person who is deluded about their lineage and ignorant of their ancestors—their noble position is merely a vain return, even though they possess necklaces.
"Meritorious virtue is in vain; what is the use of it for the future? He spoke only of the "necklace of merit," and the other two cases are to be understood by analogy.

Therefore, he concludes by saying, "The characteristics of phenomena are applied in vain, completely deluded regarding their source. Although the "rustic guest" understands this, he further warns the rest;
thus it is said: "Should one suddenly encounter such as these"—the meaning is that even if, in a future life, one should encounter such heterodox views, one should likewise [reject them].
When Shang Rong and others questioned him regarding his intent, the gains and losses concerning the Great and Small Vehicles could be understood from this:

he had already lost the Small Vehicle, as previously mentioned in the sections on "further losing the Small Truth" and "further obscuring the Small Vehicle. Thus it is said, "as has already been explained above."
The guest said, "This error is common; may I hear the explanation of the meanings of the Four Teachings as revered by you, O Benevolent One?

I replied, "These four interpretations encompass the five periods and contain within them the eight teachings; they include all the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
How could one hastily discuss their beginning and end? The guest said, "If that is so, could you perhaps explain them by means of the four..."
The teaching briefly judges whether the Buddha-nature exists or not within the insentient, and whether it is created by the mind or transformed by the mind, and whether it is complete or incomplete.

I replied: "To briefly indicate the general direction is sufficient for now. Why? Because prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the three vehicles of the *Āgama* and *Abhidharma* schools had not yet received the teaching on the nature (Buddha-nature).

Those of the Two Vehicles were intimidated by the teaching, while Bodhisattvas did not practice it. For the individual [Bodhisattva] at the initial stage, the teaching was provisional while the principle was real; thus, by means of the provisional teaching,"
Therefore, because what they have received is not yet complete, these seven types of beings may be called "insentient" (*nir-citta*), but not "without nature.

Only those of perfect capacity (*pariniṣpanna-pudgala*) know from beginning to end that principle is non-dual and that there is no realm outside the mind. Who, then, is insentient? In the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, nothing is excluded:

grasses, trees, and the earth—how do these differ from the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*)? Every step upon the long journey leads toward the Jewel Island; a mere snap of the fingers brings about union.

Since Master Xiancheng established the causes for attaining Buddhahood and granted permission for the three [categories of beings], how could his original intent have been at odds with this up until today?

To claim that insentient things lack [the capacity for enlightenment] is clearly a mistake; once this error is identified, one knows it was not a distinct insight. He then further requested that the four teachings be employed to provide a definitive judgment.

Only two [factors] act as creators across all four [types of arising]; thus, while the term "creator" (kāraka) applies generally to the Hīnayāna—where such terminology exists despite lacking its corresponding transformation—the principle of creation differs.

although the names are identical, there are commonalities and differences regarding the existence of the creator, and the objects created likewise differ in meaning.
This also differs slightly from the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings regarding the construction of karma and afflictions.

According to the distinct and perfect [teachings], the transformation and creation according to conditions—whether simultaneous or not, and whether identical or different—refers to the co-creation of the *yibao* (retributive environment), which is the shared karma of the six destinies within the realm of suffering of the three worlds.

Because sentient beings are deluded, although there are such differences as mentioned above, they are none of them but phenomena produced by correct causes and conditions. They are not [self-existent].

The "sentient beings and Buddhas of the ten directions" are precisely my own mind; this refers to their narrowness and pervasiveness.

Yet, it specifically speaks of "one thought-moment" because this reveals the perfect meaning of the "single word": that things are neither before nor after, but are possessed simultaneously.

Thus, among the contemplative methods of the Four Teachings, there is the gradual method of analyzing phenomena (*vibhajya-dharma*) and the method of penetrating the essence of phenomena (*tattva-dharma*).

The divergent theories regarding the mind give rise to two teachings; while the "semblance" (sima) and "distinct" (biejiao) teachings appear similar in their exposition of the "endowment" (ju), the distinct teaching does not fully elucidate it.

how much more so when the principle of the endowment pertains solely to the perfect. Regarding the meaning of the "endowment of seeds" (zhongju) and so forth, if one wishes to explain in detail the categories of nature and the like, these are the seeds.

the four eyes and two wisdoms perceive with distinctions, whereas from the first thought-moment, one relies upon the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom, taking the superior grade of the *Sāmbhogakāya* (Peaceful Light) as the substance of contemplation.

Thus, at the very stage where one perceives [the truth], the nine realms are immediately Śākyamuni, the three paths are immediately the Three Virtues (triguṇa), and there is nowhere one does not see the Buddha-nature;

It is neither existent nor non-existent, for it is so by its own nature. Why? Because both are the true mark (*dharmatā*). The nature of the true mark is such that it is inherently replete with all phenomena;

Therefore it is said: regarding the "seed-nature" (*gotra*), because the substance of this mind is fundamentally pervasive throughout all things, without separation or obstruction, and is identical to the Buddha like space, it is called "substance-quantity.

Because the substance of this mind is fundamentally and perfectly endowed with the body, land, cause, and fruit, lacking nothing and being no different between the living being and the Buddha, it is called "substance-virtue. When one uses this to compare with that, then—
While there are three aspects when pointing specifically toward True Suchness (*tathatā*), in essence, they are all but the single nature of inherent possession (*xingju*).
Those who do not understand this lose everything. Therefore, it is said that the single word "inherent possession" (*ju*) most clearly reveals the present school.
Having already demonstrated these three aspects, the Master of the Records (*jizhu*) further instructs us to demonstrate how practice is established based on understanding.

Relying on this, one takes the Three Jewels of the One Body as the object of focus; based on this, one gives rise to the four great vows of non-action and proceeds to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Furthermore, one causes each of these to be directed toward the rational nature (li-xing).

As for the "three causes," they refer to the sublime objects of the Three Jewels that serve as the focal point: because delusion and enlightenment share the same source, and sentient beings and Buddhas are of one essence, one relies upon this.

When one initiates practice, the six perfections and the myriad deeds are each and every one without effortful action (*anābhoga*). By means of these mountain-like practices, one fills the ocean of vows;
as practice and vows support one another, in future lives one shall ultimately attain the supreme fruit.

As for the statement, "As previously heard, the planting [of seeds] must necessarily continue," this refers to the fact that from the moment one hears the Dharma, the various [seeds] will necessarily continue.

Regarding the two ways of receiving the precepts, both are urgent; one must not lose the opportunity for human or celestial rebirths or the assemblies of Buddhas, so that one may hear [the teaching] again and attain liberation.

For those who have already received the teachings on expedient means, whether they hear them, practice them, subdue their afflictions, or sever them, the text points out the inherent perfection of the essence according to what each has attained.
Thus the Sūtra says, "That which you practice is the Bodhisattva path," as expressed in the five chapters of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

In the "Exposition of the Provisional" (Kaiquan), each instance simply states that "all these dharmas are for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle," so that upon hearing this, sentient beings all attain the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñajñāna).
This person has already received the provisional teaching; thus, when it says "if one hears, or practices, or subdues, or cuts off," these refer to the three teachings.
The attainments of those at the stages of inner and outer ordinary beings, as well as those of the small and middle sages, do not transcend mere emptiness and partial conventionality.

One should, according to the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and clarification, calmly observe the timing and point out the principle that the three thousand realms are inherently complete within the reality-mark (*dharmatā*).

If one says that the time for contemplation has not yet arrived, one should not be distressed by this, as it is for the sake of others that one explains [the teaching]; thus, two scriptural citations are provided.
The passage on "opening the provisional" serves as proof:
those who lecture and instruct with a distracted mind provide edification according to what is appropriate.
Although such individuals also rely on the teachings to lecture and instruct, their perfect understanding remains obscure and their internal wisdom is not clear regarding the One Vehicle.

As for the reason why my family has not yet attained the full integration of contemplation and observation, it is likely because those who follow the path of the lettered Dharma masters should also proceed with composure,
observing the timing and establishing their teachings according to what is appropriate for the occasion.
Regarding those who practice the contemplation of the mind (*cittāvalokana*), it is shown from the perspective of the mind.

Although such persons practice the contemplation of the mind until their hair turns white, they may still debate the nature of the mind, or claim that "the mind itself is Buddha," or belong to the class of those with arrogant conceit and obscure realization who do not understand that the mind is inherently endowed [with all qualities].
Because they have practiced the contemplation of the mind in a biased manner, they are made to contemplate [further].

At such times, whether to advance or refrain depends solely on one’s own mind to demonstrate the principle of the inherent perfection of the essence (*tixu*). If one understands this inherent perfection, internal contemplation will naturally become clear.
However, for those who are weary of the teachings and prone to contention, one should say to them: "By hearing [the Dharma], you have already planted the seeds; I do not dare to slight you."
Those who practice the Way equally shall all become Buddhas;
they merely do not accept the teaching out of reluctance. As for those who engage in disputes, it is because they hear the Great Dharma, which is beyond their capacity to bear;
thus they give rise to contention and slander. Such individuals should be treated as described above regarding Aśoka, Nandika, and Bhadrapāla—those who were once fierce and poisonous.
Although there is no immediate benefit, there is a distant planting of seeds; though one may fall into the lower realms due to slander, in the end one will surely attain liberation.

Therefore, at the conclusion of his judgment of the teachings (*śāsana-vibhāga*), the Great Master stated: "The Buddha-dharma is inconceivable, and its doctrinal characteristics (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) alone are difficult to understand.
Even the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas cannot fathom them, let alone ordinary worldlings who wish to judge this matter. It is like [trying to judge] a living being..."
It is like a blind person who, attempting to discern the characteristics of the solar disk and to judge all the various forms within the realm of space, claims to have attained full comprehension;

ultimately, such a thing is impossible. Therefore, the wise should each give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, reproaching themselves for the darkness of ignorance and abandoning frivolous proliferation and contentious strife.
Even the Great Master, having personally realized and judged this, remained humble toward his successors.
Now, according to the doctrinal system of this school, I have exhorted you, my son; it is not my own personal view, for you, my son, likewise follow the teaching as it has thus been transmitted.

This verse was spoken by the Great Master following the passage from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Battingting (柏庭) said: "Since he cautioned [the disciples] that the teaching should be bestowed according to their individual capacities..."
This is the Way; therefore, by means of this Way, one accords with the compliant teachings, and the Way flows and extends through future generations.

Consequently, [the author] again cites the Great Master’s text on the classification of teachings and his exhortations, using them along with his own words to instruct [the opponent], so that he may abandon his own views and follow only the principle, such that they no longer contend, forget the self to benefit others, and thus achieve the merit of transformation and guidance.
Vast indeed is the Buddha-dharma; it is the dharma of the mind. Because the dharma of the mind is subtle and wondrous, the Buddha-dharma is therefore inconceivable.

Furthermore, the characteristics of the teachings are the manifestations by which our Buddha established his instruction according to the capacities of sentient beings. Since these karmic conditions differ, the characteristics of the teachings are difficult to understand.
As it is said: "This is the realm of all Buddhas, which even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment have not yet fully realized."
How could that which is returned as knowledge be fathomed by those of the three vehicles, whether ordinary or sagely?
Thus, there is a profound reason for our Patriarch’s clear admonitions and exhortations.
The rustic guest, filled with joy, received them upon his head; from this day forth, through eternal kalpas, he shall only uphold them and propagate them wherever he goes.

Not disobeying his honorable command, he composed his countenance, bowed twice, and withdrew with measured grace. Suddenly awakening from the dream, neither the questioner nor the respondent, nor the question asked nor the answer given, could be found at all.
The guest was filled with joy and received the command to propagate and uphold it; and in this propagation and upholding, can it be otherwise than by means of the three modes? Therefore—
That his demeanor was so composed was not merely the result of his former coarse and rugged state; it was because he had already attained gentleness and forbearance.
That his prostrations were so reverent was not merely the result of his former lack of constancy; it was because he had already attained great compassion.
And that his bearing was so serene and dignified was not merely the result of his former standing at ease; it was because he had already attained [this state].
All phenomena are empty; wherever he propagated the Dharma, he sometimes concluded with a verse, saying: "My ancestor, the Master of Piling, once spoke of dreams within a dream.
Dream-events are inconceivable and unfathomable; the root of a dream is not real—so who is it that awakens from a dream?
Both the awakening and the dreaming are non-existent; who asks, and who answers? Question and answer are utterly ungraspable, and I, too, have nothing to attain."

One may further use dreams to fulfill dream-vows and employ illusory dreams to dedicate [merit] to all sentient beings so that they together enter samādhi, wherein all is suddenly empty like a dream or a phantom.
Once the "wild guest" had received this command to propagate and uphold the dream-scene, he ceased his discourse;
yet there was nothing to be obtained. Thus, to obtain without obtaining is to obtain it within the mind—obtaining it through non-obtaining.

Having attained this, one also attains it within the mind; thus, the principles regarding the provisional and the real, and the presence or absence of Buddha-nature within the various scriptural divisions, become crystal clear within one's breast.
How, then, could there remain any doubt concerning the partiality of the provisional?
*Vajrasamādhi-śāstra-vyākhyāna*, Scroll Lower (End). Regarding the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra-vyākhyāna*:
the Lotus Dwelling (Lianju) preserves only a handwritten manuscript of the Sanskrit original by a Song dynasty scribe; that which has not yet perished is as thin as a single thread.
It was a treasure cherished by our late teacher, the Lecturer Shaojue, who desired to circulate it widely, though he did not complete this task.

My aspirations and mindfulness have remained rooted in my teacher since I first attended him and personally absorbed his teachings; for twenty years, I have never grown weary of his instruction nor ever grown tired, as if each day were but the first.
Although the trees at his tomb are now as thick as arm-pits, I have not forgotten him from the core of my heart.

Happening upon his birthday, I have carved this [inscription] to fulfill my teacher’s wish that these two texts—dealing with the beginning and the end—be bound together into a single volume for the convenience of readers. I have thus recorded this.
Xuánzhù and his two elder brothers, Xīn and Yī, convened here to further consult with venerable masters and like-minded colleagues;

after collating and reviewing [the texts], they prepared this edition for carving. The project began on the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa Day in the second month of spring, and was completed on the Buddha’s Birthday in the first month of summer of the same year. Recorded by Lú Fù.
At this time, during the latter part of the middle summer in the year of Jia-wu (1654), I have briefly composed this in response to the *Mengqiu* (Elementary Requests) to provide a basic instruction.

I respectfully submit this with the hope that, by virtue of this book, you may always encounter virtuous friends as your companions, and that just as a skilled physician swiftly clears away cataracts from the eyes,
it may likewise clear the obstructions from the ears of others.
